She exhibited every sign of strong and passionate fondness for the male She introduced her proboscis into his ears, then put it into her mouth, caressed him warmly with her trunk, and pressed against him with her body. The scene was almost like that between brothers. But the most striking and astonishing effects were produced by the Marseilles hymn. As soon as the orchestra struck up, they whistcd, uttered sounds of joy, and then melancholy intonations. They appeared to be under the fear of some expected calamity, and were preparing themselves to meet it with resolution and fortitude. The tune was again changed, and the plaintive pensive notes pioduced corresjionding cficcts. The female rested her trunk upon the floor and appeared wrapt in unappeasable grief. But interesting as the subject is, we must here conclude without referring to the music of the Syrens, or the melody of the Italians.

The secular celebration of the invention of printing was held at Haarlem on the 10th of July last, with a great pomp. The houses and streets were covered with decorations, and at half past ten an immense collection of persons met at the Great Church. The ceremonies began with several pieces of music, alter which Professor Vander Palm delivered a discourse, in which he demonstrated that Haarlem was the cradle of the art of printing, and po.nted out all the advantages which had resulted from this important discovery. The poet Tollens succeeded him in the tribune, and reccited some very appropriate verses. The assembly then adjourned to the Town Hall, from whence it marched in procession to the Hout, to inaugurate the monument which had been erected to Lawrence Koster. The poet Artzenius then recoiled a beautiful poem on the occasion of this inaugrual festival. The principal persons who engaged in the ceremony were invited to a great banquet at the residence of his Excellency the Governor of North Holland. The celebrations were continued the following day, and the whole terminated with a grand illumination. þÿ þÿ þÿ Shipwreck and Iass of Life. þÿ Wc learn from the Baltimore American, that the brig United States, Capt. DIARY OF A DRUNKARD. The following is the journal of a drunken gentleman for one week. If some part of it should occasion disgust as well as abhorence, my readers must pardon me ; for, although my desire and intention is never to violate the rules of decency, or to offend, in any respect, the sensibility or the purity of taste, yet in exposing so degrading a vice as intemperance, we can hardly avoid depicting scenes which are nauseous. Sunday þÿ nine o'clock, disturbed by the bells ringing for church : half past nine, got up> head ache as usual ; dont know how I got home last night, dare not ask my wife, for I see she looks melancholy. N. B. My coat and pantaloons appear to have been muddy, although, 1 believe, my wife has been endeavouring to clean them Sick, no appetite. þÿ Half past ten, wife and children gone tochurch, urged me to go, but don't feel composed, very dry, took some brandy and water, eleven, took another tumbler, half-past eleven, not having eaten my breakfast, drank a little more brandy and water, twelve o'clock, never have an appetite for dinner without a little took some brandy and water, half past twelve, dinner, brandy all out, and sent Mary for another bottle, wife begged me not to send to the shops on Sunday, must have some brandy, can't eat without, drank only two tumblers at table, then slept till three o'clock, awoke parched with thirst, took some brandy and water, half past three, drank another tumbler, from four to six not so dry, drank but two or three times. Evening, wife assembled the

children to read the bible, didn t like what thev read about a drunkard. I am glad, however, I am sober to-day seven o clock went out to walk, soon tired, stepped in at the sign of the and drank some thing, and passed to rest, good comply, the sat down glasses, evening in conversation and smoking a few cigars, eleven, got home without help, though from the badness of the pavement fell twice, and the streets were so confoundedly muddy almost ashamed my wife should see me. Ilall past eleven, went to bed. þÿMonday " awoke at ten, got up, head ache and sick. Took two glases of brandy to correct the nausea of the stomach, eat nothing, my wife desired I would not go out, and said kindly, I looked too unwell to be þÿabroad. Wanted to see R. met him at the sign of . After we had been at the pools, took a glass together for Mr. \y ; offered to treat us accepted, ; more company came in : all voted -, treated them in our turn ; two o'clock concluded not to go home to dinner ; called for a beefsteak ; four o'clock, waiter told me 1 had had eight glasses of grog ; 1 am sure I have drank but six; eight, a quarrel between R. G ; I interfered, got knocked down, obliged to be carried home with my lace much bruised, wife appeared distressed, but came and bathed my wound, gave me some warm tea, helped me to bed : waked in the night and found her crying. þÿTuesday rose at ten, face sore, one eye very black, head ache still hangs on rnc. þÿ Strange nothing will cure it. Wife brought me some coffee which she said she made good

on purpose for me þÿ Could not drink it till I had taken a glass of brandy ; promised my wife I would not go out to-day. From eleven to one drank four or five glasses; two, dined, after taking another forcer, no appetite ; can't

always force : three, put a patch over my eye, and went out : my wife reminded me of my promise, and I thought I saw tears in her eyes, although she turned away her face to conceal them. Went to the sign of . Wednesday þÿ nine o'clock, waked and found myself at home, lying on the bed, with my clothes and boots on, all very much soiled with street dirt, don't remember how 1 came home : very sick, foul stomach, nausea at last suddenly relieved : my wife came and helped me to shift my clothes, and put me into a clean bed. Slept comfortably, (except some bad dreams) till one p. m. ; found my wife sitting by my side, with her work. She asked me how 1 felt, and what I would have ; told her to give me a glass of brandy. She said I'd better take a little hot tea or coflee : told her pettishly to bring the brandy ; two o clock, drank two forcers, and eat a slice ol bacon ; four, at the sign of . þÿThursday found myself in a cellar by the market : don't know how or when 1 came there ; felt sick ; called for a glass ol brand) . barman said I'd had two dollars worth ol liquor already, felt for my pocket book, missed it, had a hundred dollars iu it when I came front home : no money now, barman wouldn t forcing trust, called a hack, and drove home at four p. m. : children all glad to see me, as 1 had been out so long had nothing to give them : my wile prepared me some dinnei, eat but little, couldn't bear to see her look so kindly on me, found fault with every thing she did ; could vex her. Too much to endure all this

goodnature and forbearance ol a O 'ain, and rode down to the sign ; called a ; met hack old companions. þÿFriday eleven o'clock, waked and called the waiter to bring me brandy ; thought I was at the sign of ; my wife came and asked me it 1 would have some breaklast ; told her I must have some brandy first : drank two seemed to feel better, so took some more ; my wife asked me if 1 could spare any moncv to get the children shoes: had none for her ; but didn't like to tell her 1 had lost my pocket book; twelve, a little brandy and water ; can't drink with any pleasure before my wife, so went to the sign of : six, p. m , formed a party and sat down enjoy to ourselves; twelve, company broke up; couldn't walk : believe I've drank a little too much ; got home in a hack, hackman let me tail at the door ; clumsy rascal : alarmed my w ife. Saturday þÿ ten o'clock, waked; called to know why those bells are ringing. Mary told me 'twas meeting time ; told her it could not be Sunday, lor I had kept a journal, an 1 noted every dav in the week. Mary with her saucy impertinence, said that all one day I was not myself.

SOCIETY DETRIMENTAL TO GENIUS. Society and genius are incompatible, and the latter can rarely, if ever, be in close or frequent contact with the former, without degenerating ; it is otherwise with wit and talent, which arc excited and brought into play by the fricton of society, which polishes and sharpens both. 1 judge from personal experience, and as some portion of genius has been attributed to me, I suppose I may, without any extraordinary vanity, quote my ideas on this subject. Well, then, (continued Byron) if I have any genius, (which I grant is problematical), all I can say is, that 1 have always found it fade away, like snow before the sun, when 1 have been living much in the world. My ideas became dispersed and vague, I lost the power of concentrating my thoughts, and became another þÿbeing you will perhaps think a better, on the principle that any change in me must be for the better ; but no þÿ instead of this, I became worse, for the recollection of former mental power remained, reproach ing me with present inability, and increased the natural irritability of my nature. It must be this consciousness of diminished power that renders old people peevish, and, I suspect the peevishness will be in proportion to former ability. Those who have once accustomed themselves to think and reflect deeply in solitude, will soon begin to find society irksome; the small money of conversation will appear insignificant, after the weighty metal of thought to which they have been

used, and like the man who was exposed to the evils of poverty while in possession of one of the diamonds in the world which, from its size, could find no purchaser, such a man will find himself in society unable to change his lofty and profound thoughts into the conventional small-talk of those who surround him. þÿ Conversations of Lord Byron with the Countess of Blessington.

Exemplary Honesty. þÿ At tlie present time, when a spirit speculation and gain of has gone abroad, and a principle of strict justice in our intercourse with one another seems to be wanting, it is peculiarly gratifying to record the following instance of uncommon moral rectitude. Some few years since, a very respectable firm in Boston, Sewall, Williams, & Co., consisting of Joseph Sewall, John Williams, and Thomas It Sewall, obtained a loan from the Newburyport Bank of five thousand dollars, and gave their note, with Messrs. Walley and Foster as endorsers. About the same time Messrs. Walley and Foster also obtained a loan of five thousand dollars, for which they gave their note, with Sewell, Williams & Co. endorsers. Sometime after the loan both firms failed in business, and made assignments of their property for the benefit of their creditor's. The Newburyport Bank became a party to both assignments, and on the receipt of the final dividend of the effects of Messrs, Sewall, Williams, & Co. by the terms of the assignment, they were discharged from the note and their endorsement, and the note was delivered up to them, having a balance unpaid of about eight hundred dollars. By the assignment of Walley & Foster, their persons were to be exempt from arrest, but any property subsequently acquired by them might be taken to discharge the balance of the note. After receiving the last dividend of the effects of Walley &. Foster, between seven and eight hundred dollars remained due. Soon after

the above transaction, the charter of the Newburyport Bank expiied, and closing its concerns, among the notes sold was that of Walley & Foster, which was bid off at Auction for twenty dollars, and the purchaser delivered it to Messrs Walley & Foster for one hundred dollars. About a year since a final dividend was made among the stockholders, and as no property or legal claims were known to exist, it wai presumed there could be no further dividend. In the course of the last month a letter was received, directed to the President and Directors of the Newburyport Bank, and subscribed by Joseph Sewall, John Williams, & Thomas K. Sewall, stating that the balance unpaid on their note, and authorizing the President and Directors to draw for the amount. This was accordingly drawn for and paid. In the course of the present month, another letter was received from the same gentleman, directed to the President and Directors informing O them that as endorsers on the note of Walley & Foster, they had concluded to pay the balance unpaid on that note, and authorizing them to draw for the amount. In their letter they expressly directed that the proceeds be applied in the first place to pay any bills of the Bank which might be outstanding, and the residue to be divided among the stockholders. This sum has been drawn for and paid. There are several circumstances in the foregoing transaction which give a character peculiarly interesting. In the first place, it is not understood that these gentlemen have

come suddenly and unexpectedly into the possession of a large estate, and acted under the sudden impulse of grateful feelings, but that the above payments were the proceeds of industry and economy, and leaving them by no means in a state of affluence. In the next place it was paying to a corporation,

And again, they have paid after a full discharge by the assignment, where they were merely endorsers on a note. It may well be doubted whether any mercantile transaction in modern times can equal this nice sense of moral rectitude. It is seldom tfiat we are called up on to record a more horrible or shocking occurrence than that described in the annexed extract from a letter dated Boieville, Miss., Aug. 13, 1H35 ; þÿ A most singular and tragical incident tool; place in this village, that has cast a gloom over the spirits of all the citizens and clothed one of our most respectable families iu mourning. Preparations had been for sometime making to erect a large four story mill and manufactory, in the east part of the village, and Tuesday last was appointed for the raising As it was a matter in which the public had taken a great interest, the whole populution of the surrounding country assembled, arrangements were made for a large dinner party, and a bough house was erected for the females. With a view of surprising the Women, some young men had the night previously secreted | in a thick grove of bushes, about 200 yards from the bough house, a nine pound field piece heavily loaded, intending to discharge it when | the party were seated at table Unfortunately, it was appointed directly at the opening of the bough house. Some wretch in the mean time had taken a cat, confined its legs, and placed it in the gun. When the party were seated at the table the cannon was fired. þÿ Mrs. Blakeson, the wife of the chief magistrate of the village, who was at the head of the table, had that instant risen for some purpose, when the cat struck her just below the shoulders, and passed through her body ; she

uttered a single scream, and fell lifeless into the arms of a lady who was next to her; she was a highly accomplished and interesting young lady, and the mother of seven children, the eldest being but six years old. The cat passed over the whole length of the table, upsetting several decanters and pitchers, and its head was driven through an inch board at the east end of the bough house, where it lodged ; and what is most extraordinary, although stunned and apparently dead, it has recovered, and is now alive and well ! The authorities have offered a reward of 500 dollars for the conviction of the miscreant who was the author of this diabolical piece of mischie þÿV Sta ndard.

Influence of Intellectual Excitement. Dr. Sydenham having long attended a gentleman of fortune with little or no advantage, frankly avowed his inability to render him any further service, adding at the same time, that there was a physician of the name of Robinson, at Inverness, who had distinguished himself by the performance of many remarkable cures of the same complaint as that under which bis patient laboured, and expressing a conviction that, if he applied to him, he would come back cured. This was too encouraging a proposal to be rejected : the gentleman received from Sydenham a statement of his case, with the necessary letter of introduction, and proceeded without delay to the place in question. On arriving at Inverness, and anxiously inquiring for the residence of Dr. Robinson, he found, to his utter dismay and disappointment, that there was no physician of that name, nor even hud been in the memory of any person there. The gentleman returned, vowing eternal hostility to the peace of Sydenham ; and on his arrival at home, instantly expressed his indignation at having been sent on a journey of so many hundred miles for no purpose. þÿ Well, replies Sydenham, þÿ are you better in þÿhealth? þÿ Yes, I am now quite well, hut no thanks to þÿyou. þÿ þÿNo, says Sydenham, þÿ but you may thank Dr. Robinson for cm mg you. 1 wished to send you a journey with some object of interest in view. I knew it would be of service to you ; in going you had Dr. Robinson and bis wonderful cures in
contemplation; and in returning, you were equally engaged in thinking of scolding me þÿ! þÿ Dr. Paris.

His speeches were extremely humorous, and occasioned considerable mirth ; his successors in this same line naturally endeavoured to imitate his bright example, and hence this class of itinerant quacks obtained the general appellation of Merry Andrews. þÿ Dr. Paris.

Thin Shoes. þÿ þÿ Thin shoes, an article of female dress, I am sufficient of a Goth to wish to see disused ; and 1 would replace them with those having a moderate thickness of a sole, with a thin layer of cork or felt placed within the sole. Cork is a very bad conductor of heat, and is therefore to be preferred : if it is not to be had, or is not liked, felt may be substituted for it. I think thin shoes ought not to be used, ini ss for the purpose of dancing, and then they ought only to be worn while dancing The invalid or dyspeptic ought assuredly never to wear thin shoes. And as to the common practice of changing thin shoes for warm boots, it is a practice which 1 know to be replete with danger, and "therefore to be rash and almost culpable. There is another custom, or usage, in the dress of my fair countrywomen which must be noticed here ; it is that of covering the head with a cap in the morning, and leaving it uncovered in the afternoon or evening. It is indefensible, useless, absurd and þÿdangerous. Now, if our readers do not benefit by these rules, and keep themselves us well as possible, it will neither be our fault nor that of !><. SINGULAR DISCOVERY OF A LOST CHILD. A Swiss peasant, the father of three children, took up his summer quarters in one of those chalets which the inhabitants ol the beautiful valleys of the Canton du Vaud inhabit during the period of their grazing their flocks on the mountains. He resided ihtre with his wife and three children, tin eldest of whom, eight years age, of was an idiot; tho second, aged live, was dumb ; anu me youngest was still an infant. The iuUer was one day left alone with his two brothers, anu their mother had scarcely left them when they strayed away from their little dwelling to play among the rocks. Keturniug In nit the mother could not find them, but alter a short search she succeeded in discovering two,þÿ the infant was no-where to be seen. The idiot expressed his joy in the most extravagant manner, but the little dumb tellow on the contrary, appeared overwhelmed with consternation, and the expression ol terror in his eyes, and his whole countenance, quickly excited his þÿmother sfears, She vainly endeavoured to discover the cause ol their pantomimic gestures, but could learn nothing from the mirth of the idiot or the sorrow of the dumb child. She however hoped, from the character of the gestures used by the idiot, which resembled those of a person who, to his great joy, has found something lor which he has been looking a long time, that her child had been taken away by a in-igiibour, an event which olu.ii occurred, as the little creature was much liked and caressed. But night came, and with it no news ol me

lost hope. On the following day the unhappy parents again set out to seek their son everywhere. They had not gone lur when an eagle flew over their heads, which excited anew the joy of the idiot and the terrors of the dumb boy, who pressed closely to his father, and hid his head in his hands to avoid seeing the bird. The mother then became certain that the child had been carried off by a bird of prey. In fact, on the same day that the fatal accident took place, a huntsman had stationed himself in ambuscade near an þÿeagle n s est, to wait for a shot at the bird as be approached his prey. Alter having watched for some hours with that characteristic patience which distinguishes the Swiss hunter he at length perceived one of those monarchs of the Alps approaching slowly towards the rocks, appearing twice as large as an ordinary eagle. The þÿhunter s surprise was extreme when, on a nearer approach, he saw that the bird carried a child in his talons, lie heard its cries, and

clearly distinguished its face. He had but one course to adopt, nor did he hesitate to employ it, that of shooting the eagle. He put up a prayer to God, took aim at the bird( and fired. The shot took effect, and the eagle fell dead, shot through the head The hunter recovered the child, and carried it home to the wretched and incredulous mother. The boy was dreadfully torn by the þÿeagle s talons, but none of his hurts were mortal. þÿ French Paper.

The late fire at New York is the largest tor the number of buildings and for amount of properly destroyed, which has yet occurred in the United States þÿ nearly 700 mercantile establishments were a prey to the Jlames, and 3,000 clerks, porters, engaged in them, arc deprived of employ. The fire was seen at Fhiladelpia and at New Haven, from the former (100 miles from New York) several companies offire-men started on the first alarm and were rapidly conveyed to New York on the railroads, and arrived in time to be of essential service. The Thermometer ( Farenheits ') stood at Zero (32 degrees below freezing point) the night of the five ; many bales of blankets tvere converted into cloaks by the fire-men, by cutting holes in them for their arms, and several hundred baskets of Champaigne were drank by them, ( being thrown out of the Stores on fire) to warm them. The new Exchange (built about ten years since) and two large churches, were entirely destroyed. A large pile of Dry Goods ( probably to the value of a million) was made, in I the middle of Hanover- Square (removed there

Traveling Cat. þÿ A lady residing m Glasgow had a handsome cat sent to he: from Edinburgh ; it was conveyed to her iii a muse basket, and in a carriage. She was caretuliy watched for two months, but having produced a pair of young ones at the end of that time, she was left to her own discretion, which she very soon employed in disappearing with both her kittens. The lady at Glasgow wrote to her friend at Edinburgh, deploring her loss, and the cat was supposed to have formed some new attachment, with as little reflection as men and women sometimes do. About a fortnight, however, after her disappearance at Glasgow, her well known mew was heard at the street door of her old mistress, and there she was, with both her kittens ; they in the best state, but she very thin. It is clear that she could only carry' one kitten at a time. þÿ The distance from Glasgow to Edinburgh is forty miles, so that if she broight one kitten part of the way, and then went back for the other, and thus conveyed them alternately, she must have traveled one hundred and twenty miles at least. Her prudence must likewise have suggested the necessity of journeying the night, with many other precau- in tions for the safety of her young.

Migratory Instinct of Animals þÿ A British officer on board a ship, which touched at the island of Ascension, in her way to England, informed me that they took in several large turtles, and amongst others, one, which, from some accident, had only three fins. The sailor on board called it the þÿ Lord þÿNelson, and it was marked in the usual way by having certain initials and numbers burnt upon its under shell with a hot iron, which marks are never to be obliterated. Owing to various causes the ship was delayed on her voyage; many of the turtles died, and others became sickly. This was the case of the þÿ Lord Nelson and it was so nearly dead when the ship arrived in the Channel that the sailors, with whom it was a favorite, threw it overboard, in order, as they said, to give it a chance. Its native element, however, appears to have revived it ; for two years afterwards the very same turtle was again found at its old haunts in the island of Ascension. The proofs brought forward of the accuracy o the statement place the fact beyond doubt, and afford a wonderful instance of the instinct of this fish. When we consider the vast tract of waters which this turtle had to pass, and that tire island ot Ascension is only a little speck in the ocean, it is impossible not to reflect on that unexplained instinct with wonder, which enabled so unwieldly, and apparently so stupid an animal, to find its way back to a rock in the desert of þÿwaters.

LATER FROM CANTON. By the ship Paris, Capt. Leach, from Canton, wo have papers from the Celestial Empire, to June 12th 1835. The following sensible placard was posted on the walls of Canton during the great drought. A course exhortation to arouse the age. It is really thought that it is the year of the waterkulpa. There is now a great drought ; calamities and misfortunes are heaped up ; and it is a time of sorrow and grief. Prayers are of no avail ; all (these misfortunes) proceed from ourselves. Our hearts have long been hardened, and we have been discontented with our lots : the un-eradicated roots of error are many. Evil dispositions burst out like torrents overthrowing mountains ; therefore heaven is annoyed with our repealed supplications. I offer advice to the men of age. It is necessary they should examine themselves, and let no one think himself guiltless, and accuse others. Let all at once excite their hearts, and from their own feelings conjecture those of others ; constantly be contented in your stations ; cherish with the greatest care filial duty & brotherly love ; then, the harmony of relations, friends, youth and manhood. In affairs do not indulge your own temper and wishes ; depend not on talent and ability ; presume not on riches and treat people contemptuously, and on high station to insult them. Be not covetous of illgot wealth ; think not on unlawfull pleasures ; presume not on strength and power ; cherish not revengefull feelings. In all affairs, consult

your heart and hold last by reason. Constantly correct yourselves, and be indulgent to the thoughts ol others ; certainly you will then be able to repent and renovate yourselves, and draw back the favorable will of heaven : seek and do all this with real sincerity, and it cannot be but the calamities will be changed into blessings. þÿ Going Ahead,!' þÿ A runaway couple, with their attendants, came to this city on Monday morning, and immediately crossed the river to Aberdeen, a second þÿ Gretna þÿGreen, in order to be united in the holy bonds of matrimony. The job was speedily done, and the couple pronounced þÿ man and þÿwife. The þÿbride s be vested in the hands maid, a plump and rosy little lass, at the conclusion of the ceremony, innocently said, with a winning and killing smile, þÿ that it was so easy a thing to get married, she would like to try it þÿtoo. Her partner, being too gallant to be outdone or back out, bravely determined to þÿ þÿahead, and instantly shelled out the go pre-requisite possibly þÿ a þÿ Jackson yellow þÿboy. The suddenly excited hopes were quickly swallowed up in exquisite fruition, and the couple returned to Kentucky with their companions, a delighted husband and wife. þÿ Maysville (Kij ) Eagle.

How to gel a Tight Ring off a þÿFinger. Thread a needle flat in the eye with a strong þÿ thread : pass the needle with care under the ring, and pull the thread through a few inches toward the hand ; wrap the long end of the thread tightly round the finger, regularly, all down to the nail, to reduce its size. Then lay hold of the short end of the thread, and unwind it. The thread pressing against the ring, will gradually remove the tightest ring without difficulty, howevsr swollen the finger may be.

A friendless Irish Gi/l. þÿ The coroner of Philadelphia was called on Tuesday last, to view the body of an infant, at the corner of George and Broad streets, under the following circumstances : þÿ It appeared that Isabella Ballcntine, the mother of said child, came to the house of Henry Barcklcy, as above, on the previous Wednesday, and stating that she was a stanger, requested that she might stop there a short time. The next day she gave birth to the infant above mentioned, which, for want of proper nourishment, died on Tuesday morning. Isabella said she had been in America only 6 months, that her father James Ballcntine, lived in the county of Tyron, Cookstown, Ireland, was a wealthy man, that she had been courted and promised marriage, by John Conway, of the same place, that her father said he would shoot her rather than she should marry a poor man like John Conway, and she then ranaway with Conway, but could not get married. Her father followed them with two of her brothers and a number of his tenants, and threatened to kill Conway and pull down the honse, if she was not given up. She never saw her mother or home after. She was taken on board of the ship Prudence, and sent to America, without a cent of money or a change of clothes. Her father knew her situation at the time he sent her a stranger in a strange land. She expressed a wish that he should know that her cup of misery was full to overflowing, and that she had seen the error of her ways.

The advantages of this method of communication by signal, over every other, are briefly these : þÿ fn the first place, it will be found, by fur the cheapest, the whole expense being die price of the book, which is only sixteen shillings ; the purchase of flags or other symbols being unnecessary. foreign one, and vice, versa, w ithout the least knowledge of each other's language, and under circumstances of peril and distress which have rendered every other mode impracticable. LEGHOIIN, Oct. 2, The Cholera lias nearly disappeared from amongst us ; in fact, it made no progress, and the character of the disease was much less intense than in other places. The greater number of those attacked have recovered. þÿ Yesterday there were seven new cases and only one death. The French Steamer, the Miediterranean, has resumed her voyages between this city and Marseilles. Three Portuguese ships of war, which had been for some time stationed along the coast of Genoa and latterly in the bay of Spezzia, have come to anchor in our roads, in consequence of the misunderstanding, between the Portuguese and Sardinian Governments.

Royal Marriages. þÿ A letter of the 7th of Oct. from Frankfort has the following : þÿ " It is 'aid, that during the conferences at Toplitz two marriages were proposed, with a view of drawing still closer the alliance between Russia, Prussia, and Austiia. The Emperor Nicholas has demanded for his son, the hereditary Prince, who is about 18, the hand of the Archduke Charles's daughter, who is 17, and offered to unite his daughter, the Princess Olga, with Prince William, the King of Prussia's nephew. These plans, however, have, it is rumored, met with obstacles. King Frederick William, on the proposal being made to him, inquired whether Prince William might not, on his union with the Princess Olga, obtain that part of the kingdom of Poland which is under the sceptre of the Czar? This suggestion seemed to be Very displeasing to the Emperor Nicholas, who has no intention of relinquishing his hold on Poland, neither have the Poles any greater desire to bo under the direction of a Prussian Prince than to remain under that of Russia. þÿ The Archduke Charles hn« frequently assured his daughter, that she should not be sacrifn cd to political views, and that she should be allowed to consult her own feelings in the choice of a husband. The Princess Theresa does not appear to have any inclination to live in Russia, and if she should refuse the hand of a Russian Prince, she w ill certainly not offend her father."

On the 24th Sept. the anniversary of the death of Ron Pedro was celebrated at Lisbon, with mournful pomp. From daylight to sunset all the ships of-war and batteries fired every live minutes. The flags were hoisted halfmast, and the yards were crossed obliquely at acute angles: and though the weather was very unfavourable, the Queen, the corps diplomatique, 1 lie ministers, and officers of both services, and a vast concourse of civilians, attended the high mass performed for the repose of his soul at the convent church of San Vincent do Fora, where bis mortal remain are buried. The Empress, bis interesting widow, was prevented by indisposition from attending, but heard mass that morning at the chapel of the palace of Neccssidades

The affair of the marriage of the Queen of Portugal makes progress At a cabinet council held at Lisbon on the 25th Sept. it is said to have been agreed to sign the contract for the Queen's union with a Prince of Saxe Coburg Gothu, a younger brother at Leopold King of Belgium.

The domestic news presents but few subjects of consequence, and these may be principally comprised in the arrival at Dover, of the King and Queen of the Belgians, and the commemoration of the third centenary of the Bible, throughout England, on the 4th last month þÿ it being, we are told, that day three hundred yeais when the completion of the translation of the Iloly Scriptures into the English language took place. The visit of the King and Queen of Belgium is pronounced free from any political motive, having, as it is believed, no other object than the introduction of his young consort to those persons whom he regards in both countries. Her Royal Highness the Duchess of Kent and the Princess Victoria, accompanied their Majesties on their way to the town oi Ramsgate þÿ the inhabitants of which presented appropriate, dutiful and loyal addresses to the Princess and her Royal Highness, and also addresses of congratulation were presented to Prince Leopold and his Queen, which were answered in a correspondent tone. The West India interests, it is stated would receive a considerable portion of their claims on the 5th last month. We are sorry to perceive that the cry of agricultural distress throughout the United Kingdom is represented to be as ' loud and deep" as ever. The farming interests arc considered in a deplorable state of depression ; although the government, it appears, does not sympathize in this distress, his Majesty, we are told, feels it deeply. The Marquis of

Chandos, at a public meeting of agriculturists and farmers, some short time ago, assured them that the Sovereign looked upon their interests with the greatest solicitude and was extremely anxious for the restoration of the farmers prosperity þÿ an epoch which, it is feared, will never arrive, at least so long as these suffering classes are mocked with the Malthusian and anti-christian Poor Law Bill> as a measure of efficient relief. Our Island Agent has very recently been in personal communication with the Secretary for the Colonics, at his Lordship's official place of business. The Standard informs us that Lord Spencer has been asked by the Premier to take office, but positively refused to join the administration, or have any thing to do with Mr. O'Connell. The same authority states, that Mr. O'Loghlen, the Whig Radical Attorney General for Ireland, has been sworn in as Privy Councillor, and that Mr. O'Conncli now fills, by deputy , the four important offices of Lord Lieutenant, Chief Secretary, Attorney-General and Privy Councillor. The great agitator appears to be the cause of much envy or great fear to the good people of England. Captain Back, the intrepid Polar navigator, has been promoted to the rank of Post Captain, as a reward for his extraordinary service. The Stanmer packet conveyed to his Majesty's Government information uf the Barbados House of Assembly having passed the various measures recommended by bis Excellency the Governor General ; but their late

Danger of Flying Kites in the Streets. Tuesday an inquest was held at the London Hospital, in the Mile End-road, on the body of Robert Coble, a youth of 1 7 years of age, who died in the Hospital on Sunday last It appeared from the evidence that the deceased, who was in the employment of Mr. Abbott, a cow-keeper at Limchouse, while driving a horse and cart belonging to his master, the animal took fright through some boys flying a kite in the street, and ran of! at a furious rate. The deceased, in endeavouring to control him, fell down, and the wheel passed over him, inflicting the most severe injuries on his abdomen and loins. He was instantly carried to the hospital, where he lingered until the following day. A verdict of Accidental Death was returned þÿ Observer, Sept 27.

A SINGULAR ADVENTURE. Once upon a time, a traveller stepped into a stage coach. He was a young man starting in life. He found six passengers about, him, all greyheaded, and extremely aged men. The youngest appeared to have seen, at least, eighty winters. Our young traveller, struck with the singularity mild and happy aspect which distinguished all his fellow passengers, determined to ascertain the secret of a long life, and art of making old age comfortable ; he addressed the one who was apparently the eldest, who told him that he had always led a regular and abstemious life, eating vegetables and drinking water. The young man was rather daunted at this, inasmuch as he liked the good things of this life. þÿ He addressed the second, who astounded him by saying that he had always eaten roast beef, and gone to bed regularly fuddled for the last seventy years, adding, that all depends upon regularity The third had prolonged his days by never seeking or accepting office ; the fourth, by resolutely abstaining from all political or religious controversies, and the fifth by getting to bed at sunset and rising at dawn. The sixth was apparently much younger than the other five þÿ his hair was less grey, and there was more of it þÿ a placid smile, denoting a perfectly easy conscience, mantled his face, and his voice was jocund and strong. They were all surprised to learn that he was by tea years the oldest man in the coach. " How," exclaimed our young traveller, "how is it that you have preserved the freshness of life ?" I

have drank water and wine þÿ I have eaten meat and vegetables I have held a public þÿ office þÿ I have dabbled in politics, and written in religious pamphlets þÿ I have sometimes gone to bed at midnight, got up at sunrise and noon but always paid promptly Jur r j þÿ I newspapers."

Anecdote of Lohenxo Dow. þÿ D following anecdote of this eccentric cli r.eter has been sent us in manuscript by a correspondent, who thinks it has never been published. At any rate, it i» worth republishing. þÿ Some years since, Lorenzo preached in Charleston, South Carolina, and in the course of one of bis sermons, attacked with some severitx the character of a citizen w ho had lateconsequence of his vices, l'or this ly died, and whose death he alleged was at he was in the instance of the relatives of the deceased, court sentenced him to pay a small tine, prosecuted and found guilty by jury, arid a i bo endure a short imprisonment, i he Governor of the State, however, pardoned him and paid the fine himself. Substitute for Steam. þÿ The following plan has been addressed by Mr. John Galt to the editor of the Greenock Advertiser; þÿ þÿ Take a cylinder and subjoin to the bottom of it, in communication, a pipe þÿ fill the pipe and the cylinder with water þÿ in the cylinder place a piston as in that of the steam-engine, and then with a Bramah's press, and a simple obvious contrivance which the process will suggest, force the water up the pipe, the pressure of which will raise the piston. This is the demonstration of the first motion. Second: When the piston is raised, open a cock to discharge the water, and the piston will descend. This is the demonstration of the second motion, and is as complete as the motion of the piston in the cylinder of the steam engine, and a power is attained as effectual as steam, without risk of explosion, without the cost of fuel, capable of being applied to any purpose in which steam is used, and to an immeasurable extent. The preservation of the water may, in some cases, be useful, and this may be done by a simple contrivance, viz ; þÿ by making the cock discharge into a conductor, by which the water may be conveyed back at every stroke of the piston, into the pipe, at the end of which the þÿBramah p s ress þÿacts.

Lord þÿExmouth Early s Daring þÿ Active beyond his companions, Mr. Pellew did the þÿship sduty with a smartness which none of them could equal ; and as every one takes pleasure where he excels, he had soon become a seaman. At the same time the buoyancy of youth, and a natural playful disposition, led him continually into feats of more than common daring. In the spring of 1775 General Burgoyne took his passage to America in the Blonde, and when he came alongside, the yards were manned to receive him. Looking up, he was surprised to see a midshipman on the yard-arm standing on his head. Captain Pownal, who was at his side, soon quieted Ins apprehensions by assuring him that it was only one of the usual frolics of young Pellew, and that the General might make himself quite at ease for his safety, for that if he should fall, he would only go under the þÿship s bottom and come up on the other side. What on this occasion was probably spoken but in jest, was afterwards more than realized, for he actually sprang from the fore-yard of the Blonde, where she was going fast through the water, and saved a man who had fallen overboard. Captain Pownall reproached him for his rashness, but he shed tears when he spoke of it to the officers, and declared that Pellew was a noble fellow. þÿ Osiers life of Lord Exmoulh.

Advertising for þÿH iees þÿ Until the present time, we have had no faith in the efficacy of this modern system of making overtuies of matrimony, but on the contrary believed it to be an idle and absurd practice, and used only for sport or mischief. VYre have now, however, cause for a different belief, inasmuch as the young man who advertised in the Transcript during the last week lor a wife, has, in consequence of such publication, succeeded in entering into a solemn connubial engagement with a fair young lady residing in the upper part of the city, and is to be married on Friday next. Moonshine. þÿ The gullible portion of the reading community have been consummately hoaxed by an article which appeared, last week in the New York Sun, purporting to be extracted from a supplement to the Edinburgh ; Journal of Science, and communicating intelligence of stupendous discoveries in the Moon, made by Sir John Herschel, from his observatory on the Cape of Good Hope þÿ effected by the assistance of a new telescope of immense power, which brought the planet within forty miles of the eye of the observer, and rendered objects, not more than twenty two yards in diameter, distinctly visible. Nearly half the article, is employed in a description of the monstrous telescope which has effected these wonders, and the history of its origin and progress of construction. It is written in a scientific vein, which mocks gravity, and evinces much learning, acumen, and deep observation þÿ blended with a satirical propensity, that marks the author as no ordinary man. þÿ Uuubcc Mercury .

Singular Anecdote of a Dog. þÿ A gentleman now residing in London, whilst travelling outside of one of the north mails, was witness of the fact I am about to relate It was a dark night, and as the mail was travelling at the usual rate, a dog barked incessantly before the leaders, and continued to do so for some time, jumping up to the heads of the horses. The coachman, fearful of some accident, pulled up, and the guard got down to drive the animal away. The dog ran before the guard, and then returned to him, making use of such peculiar gestures, that he was induced to take out one of the lamps and follow the dog. After doing so for one hundred yards, he found a farmer lying drunk across the road, and his horse "razins; by the side of it. But for this extraordinary sagacity and affection of the dog for his master, the coach would most probably have been driven over the body of tho sleeping man.

THE LOST ONE. A Live-oaker," employed 011 the St. John's " River, in East Florida, left his cabin, situated 011 the banks of that stream, and with his axe on his shoulder, proceeded toward the swamp in which he had several times before allied his trade of felling and squaring the giant trees that afford the most valuable timber for naval architecture and other purposes. At the season which is thebest for this kind of labor, heavy fogs not frequently cover the country, so as to render it difficult for one to see farther than thirty or forty yards in any direction. The woods, too, present so little variety, that every tree seems the mere counterpart every of other ; and the grass, when it has not been burnt, is so tall, that a man of ordinary stature cannot see over it, whence it is necessary for him to proceed with great caution, lest he should unwillingly deviate from the ill defined trail which he follows. þÿ To increase the difficulty, several trails often meet, in which case unless the explorer be perfectly well acquainted with the neighborhood, it would be well for him to lie down and wait until! the fog should disperse. Under such circumstances, the best woodsmen are not unfrequently bewildered for a while; and I well remember that such an occurrence happened to myself, at a time when I had imprudently ventured to pursue a wounded quadrupedj which led me to some distance from the track. The live-oaker had been jogging onwards for several hours, and became aware that he

must have travelled considerable more than the distance between his cabin and the " hammock," which he desired to reach. To his alarm, at the moment when the fog dispersed, he saw the sun at its meridian height, and could not recognize a single object around him. Young, healthy, and active, he imagined that he walked with more than usual speed, and had passed the place to which he was bound. He accordingly turned his back upon the sun, and pursued a different route, guided by a small trail. Time passed, the sun heeded his course ; he saw it gradually descend in the west ; but ail around him continued as if enveloped with mystery. The huge grey trees spread their giant boughs, a living being crossed his path, all was silent and still, and the scene was like a dull and dreary dream of the land of oblivion. He wandered like a forgotten ghost that had passed into the land of spirits, without yet meeting one of his kind with whom to hold converse. The condition of a man lost in the woods is one of the most perplexing that can be imagined by a person who has not himself been in a like predicament. Every objict he sees, he first thinks he recognizes, and w hile his whole mind is bent on searching for more than may gradually lead to his extrication, he goes on committing greater errors the further he proceeds. This was the case with the live oaker. The sun was now setting with a fiery aspect, and by degrees it sunk in its full circular form, as if giving warning of a sultry morrow. þÿ

Myriads of insects delighted at its departure, now filled the air on huzzing wings. Each piping frog arose from the muddy pool in which it had concealed itself: and the squirrel retired to his hole, the crow to his roost, arid, far above, the harsh croaking voice of the

heron announced, that full of anxiety, it was wending its way to the miry interior of some distant swamp. Now the woods began to resound to the shrill cries of the owl : and the breeze, as it swept among the columnar streams of the forest trees, came laden with heavy and chilling dews. Alas, no moon with her silvery light shone on the dreary scene, and the lost one, wearied and vexed, laid himself down on the damp ground. Prayer is always consolatory to man, in every difficulty or danger, and the woodman firmly prayed to his Maker, wished his family a happier night than it was his lot to experience, and with a feverish anxiety, waited the return of day. You may imagine the length of that cold dull, moonless night. With the dawn of day came the usual fogs of those latitudes. The poor man started' on his feet, and, with a sorrowful heart, pursued a course which he thought might lead him to some familiar object, although, indeed, he scarcely knew v. ha! ho was doing. No longer had he the trace of a track to guide him, and yet as the sl.ii rose, he calculated the many hours of day light he had before him, and the farther he went, continued to walk the faster. But vain were all his hopes ; that day was spent in fruitless adventures to regain the path that led to his home, and when night again approached, tire terror that had been gradually spreading over his mind, together wilh the nervous debility induced by fatigue, anxiety, and hunger, rendered him almost frantic. He told me, that

at this moment he beat his breast, tore his hair, and, had it not been for the piety with which his parents had, in early life, imbued his mind, and which had become habitual, would have cursed his existence þÿ Famished, as he now was, he laid himself 011 the ground, and fed on the weeds and grass that grew around him. That night was spent in the greatest ;n ay and terror. þÿ " 1 knew my situation," he s. i i tome. "I was fully aware, that unless Almighty God came to my assistance, i must perish in those uninhabited woods. 1 knew that 1 had walked more than fifty milt s, although I had not met with a brook, from wh en I could quench my thirst, or even alias the buining heat of my parched lips and hi od shot eyes. I knew, that if 1 should not meet with some stream, 1 must die, for my axe was my only weapon, and although deers and bears now and then started within a few yards, or even feet of me, not one ol them coulu 1 kill ; and although I was in the midst of abundance, not a mouthful did 1 expect to procure, to satisfy the crav ings of my empty stomach. Sir, may God preserve you from ever feeling ' as I did the whole of that day ! For several days after, no one can imagine the condition in which he was, for when he related to me this painful adventure, he assured me that he had lost all recollection of what had happened. " God," he continued "must have taken pity on me one day : for, as I ran wildly through those dreadful pine barrens, I met with a tortoise. I gazed upon it with

amazement, and delight, and although I knew, that were 1 to follow it undisturbed, it would lead me to some water, my hunger and thirst would not allow me to refrain from satisfying both, by eating its flesh and drinking its blood. With one stroke of my axe, the beast was cut in two, and in a few moments, I depatched all but the shell. Oh, Sir, how much 1 thanked God, whose kindness had put the tortoise in my way ! I felt greatly renewed. I sat down at the foot of u pine, gazed on the heavens,

3 &TX3 thought of my wife and children, and again and again thanked my God for my life, for, know, 1 felt less distracted in my mind, and more assured, that before long, 1 must recover my way, and get back to my home." The Lost One remained, and passed the night, at the foot of the same tree, under which his repast had been made. Refreshed by sound sleep, he started at dawn to resume his weaiy march. The sun rose bright, and lie followed the direction of the shadows. Still, the dreariness of the woods was the same, and he was on the point of giving up in despair, when he observed a rackoon lying squatted on the grass. Raising his axe he drove it with such violence through the helpless animal, that it expired without a struggle. What he had done with the turtle, he now did with the rackoon, the greater part of which he actually devoured at one meal. With more comfortable feelings, he then resumed his wanderings þÿ his journey, 1 cannot say, for although in the possession of all his faculties, and in broad day light, he was worse off than a lame man groping his way in the dark out of a dungeon, of which he knew not where the door stood. Days one after another, passed þÿ nay, weeks in succession. He fed now on cabbage trees, then on frogs and snakes. All that fell in his way was welcome and savory. Yet he became daily more emaciated, until at length he could scarcely crawl. Forty days had elapsed, by his own reckoning, when he at last reached the banks of the river. His clothes in tatters, his once bright axe dimmed with

rust, his face begrimmed with beard, his hair matted, and his feeble frame little better than a skeleton covered with parchment : there he laid himself down to die. Amid the perturbed dreams of his fevered fancy, he thought he heard the noise of oars far away on the silent river, lie listened, but the sound died away in his ear. It was indeed a dream, the last glimmer expiiing hope, and now the light of of life was about to lie quenched for ever. þÿ But again the sound ol oars awoke him from his lethargy, lie listened soeagerly, that the hum oi a flv could nut have escaped his ear. They were mdeed the measured boats of oars, and now, joy to the forlorn soul ! the sound of human voices thrilh d to his heart, and awoke the tumultuous pulses of returning hope, (in h s knees did the eye ol God see that man bv the broad std' stream that glittered in the sunbeams, tun! human eyes soon saw him too, for reel .1 t headland covered with tangled brt aw ,1 boldly advances the little boat, polled by its lusty rower. The Lost One raises Ins let hie voice on high : þÿ it was a loud shrill sere. 111 of joy and tear. The row rs panst , and look aiound. Another, but feebler screii in, and they ol serve him. It comes þÿ Ins 1 e 0 et iii it if s, i f, sight is dimmed, his Drain tee :sps loi breath. It comes, þÿ it has in , on the beach, and the Lost Cue is found. This is a tale of no fiction, hut the relation of an arte; occui reiice, which might be cmbob : > ed, no (iout t, but which is better in the

plain gai n of truth. The notes by which 1 rerouted it, were written m the cabin of the once lost, live-oaker, at out lour years after the painful incident occurred. llis amiable wife and loving children, were present at the recital, and never shall I forget the tears that flowed from them as they listened to it, albeit it had long been more familiar to them than a tale thrice told. .Sincerely do 1 wish, pood rcaucr, that neither you tier 1 may i ver elicit such sympathy, by having undergone such suhi rings, although, no doubt, such svmpathy would be a rich recompense for them. It only remains for me to say that the distance betwci n the cal in and the live-oak hammock to which the woodman was bound, scarcely exceeded 8 miles, while the part of the river at which he was found, was. miles from the house. Calculating his dailv wanderings at It) miles, we may believe, that tin v amounted in all to 4(d). He must, therefore, have rambled in a circuitous direction, which people generally do in such circumstances. Nodal but the great strength of his constitution, and the merciful aid of his Maker, have supported him for so long a time.

Tiie Napoleon Family. þÿ The son of the King Holland of lias addressed the following letter to the Editor of the National : þÿ " Sir, þÿ Several journals have noticed the report of my departure for Portugal, as a pretender to the hand of Queen Donna Maria. However flattering to me he the supposition of an union with a young, beautilul, and virtuous Queen, the widow of a cousin who was dear to me, it is my duty to refute such a report, since no step that I am acquainted with can have given rise to it. 1 must even add that, notwithstanding the lively interest attached to the destinies of a people that has just acquired its liberties, I should refuse the honour of sharing the throne of Portugal, if chance made some persons cast their eyes upon me. The noble conduct of my father, who, in 1810, abdicated because he could not combine the interests of France with those of Holland, has not been obliterated from my mind. My father has proved to me by his great example, how preferable our native country is to a foreign throne. I feel that, accustomed from my infancy to cherish my country above all, I can prefer nothing to the interests of France. þÿ Persuaded that the great name I bear will not always be a title of exclusion in the eyes of my countrymen, since it reminds them of 15 years of glory, I await with calmness, in a hospitable and free country, that the people recall to their bosom those whom in 1815, twelve hundred thousand foreigners banished. This hope of one day serving France as a
citizen and a soldier, invigorates my soul, and is worth, in my estimation, all the thrones in the world. þÿ I am &c., Napoleon Lous Buonaparte. þÿ Arenenburg December 14, 1835."

Most Extraordinary Event. The Mona's Herald, of Friday week, con tains the particulars of a very extraordinary event which has occurred in the Isle ol Man. A man and his wife arrived, early in the year 1833, on the island from Scotland, accompanied by the woman's daughter by a former husband. The child, it is stated, was entitled, by her father's will, to the sum ol ill 000; and her brother, who remained with his lather's relations, to that ol £6000. The woman was in narrow circumstances, and, it is supposed, had fixed his eyes on the child's portion. But how to gain his object was a puzzle. At the latter end of the year 1833, the little girl, who had been her mother's darling, sickened, and, alter a week's illness, to all appearance died. The body, it was supposed, was buried in the church-yard ot Kirk Bride, the usual ceremony having been performed by the Rev. Mr. Nelson. The man, as a matter of course, communicated the tidings of the death of the child, accompanied with the clergyman's certificate ot her tuneral, to the guardians in Scotland, who were, consequently, bound to pay him, in his wile s behalt, the £1000 settled upon the child by the will of her father. Whether he received the whole of the money or not, is uncertain it is : said, however that he received £100, and left the island, last summer, for Ireland Suspicion seems to have existed as to the fate of the child ; and the neighbours who had assisted at the funeral requested the clergyman to give them permission to open the grave. Ac-
cordingly, on Saturday morning se'nnight, the Rev. Mr. Nelson and others proceeded to the grave, had it opened, and, on removing

the lid of the coffin, found þÿ what? a log of wood, which purported to form the body, and two pieces of sticks, intended to represent the legs! The effigy was regularly attired in grave clothes, had a cap on the head, and a fine cambric frill round the neck, Wiiat become of the little girl remains to be discovered.

Eloquence of Wine. þÿ On an occasion, when Matthews was returning very late, or, by'r lady, it might be early in the morning, to Edinburgh, his friend, who was somewhat fou, refused to pay the toll, stating that he had paid it before that day. The little girl locked the toll ; and he loaded her with abuse, to which she made little reply. After much alteration, her mother opened a casement above, and in a sleepy, feeble tone, inquired what the gentleman said. "Na, mither," said the child, it's no the gentleman, it's the wine " speaking."

The following is a curious and we believe novel account of the circumstances attending the marriage of Colonel Lennox with Lady Charlotte Gordon, shortly after his duel with the Duke of York. It is extracted from the lately published biography of one of the servants of the Gordon family : þÿ ' Before we left London, as I learned afterwards, the Dutchess of Gordon had sent orders to Gordon Castle, confidentially, concerning the marriage-ceremony. It was arranged that the housekeeper should have a certain clergyman in attendance when we þÿarrived. The ceremony took place in the durhess'g best dressing-room. The duke was not at home. No body in the house but the duchess and two women-servants, besides the immediate parties, knew of the wedding, not even the Marquess of Huntly, Lady Charlotte's brother, till the third day after. The reason, I believe, was to avoid tedious parade. On the morning of the third day the duchess informed her son, the Marquess ot Huntly, of the event. As a great number of the neighbouring gentry, according to custom, had assembled to welcome the arrival of the family into the North, the young marquess was very desirous of being himself the instrument to announce the news. Accordingly, after dinner was over, and the ladies had retiied, the marquess, archly addressing Col. Lennox, said, ' Coionel, allow us to drink Charlotte's health in style ' ' Stay,' said the colonel, 'let us first get her grace's leave.' He directly left the room, and returning in a short time,

announced to the young marquess, that 4 the duchess gave consent ' 4 Then,' said the marquess. let it be in bumpers.' 4 4 Nay,' said the colonel, 4 let us have bottles, and give me two!' So said, so done : each gentleman had a bottle set before him, with the cork ready drawn, and Colonel Lennox two, as he had desired. þÿ The colonel then rose from his seat, and gave, in a bold and unfaltering voice, 4 Lady Charlotte Lennox !' A burst of astonishment and applause was the consequence. The servants in waiting directly communicated it to those without, and every part of the house literally rang with the news as it flew from room to room. I believe every man at the table drank his bottle of wine in due style, and the bridegroom his two. As the bottles wVre emptied, they laid them on the table, each one with its neck to a common centre, and thus made the form of a star in honour of the ceremony, " which remained till next day

The ball pierced the Thus has been revealed a body, which þÿ in spite of ail known and imagined causes of orbital derangement, during its immense course through all the vicissitudes of light and darkness, heat and cold, þÿ returned within eight or nine days of its appointment, in upwards of 76 years; and even this slight irregularity is more imputable to errors of observations than of investigation, for there were many sources of error that the most skilful astronomers could not avoid, before the perfecting of instruments to the degree which they have now arrived at. This happy fulfilment of a wonderful prediction, is a glorious triumph to science, and one equally gratifying to geometers, computers, observers, and opticians ; for the indubitable proof of its belonging to our system, opens objects so new and important, that Halley prophetically expected that "candid posterity would not refuse to acknowledge it was first discoveied by an Englishman." þÿ before the periodicity of this comet was established, there were many philosophers, and some of them of no mean note, who argued against the whole cometory theory, maintaining that they were mere accidental bodies falling through the regions of space, having no dependence on our sun, or connexion with our system. A Rum þÿStory. Mr. Hunt of North Carolina, said, at a Temperance Meeting at New York, not long since, that the lovers of rum are distinguished for inventing modes to obtain it. In illustration, he said a man in Orange country, North Carolina, came home with a keg of rum, but was immediately summoned to attend court as a juror, and he was greatly puzzled to know what to do with his rum, for his wife being an intemperate woman, would find it though he should hide it. He finally lashed a strap around it, and suspended it from a beam above the good wife's reach she being lame and infirm, was supposed unable to get at the rum. After he was gone, she placed the wash-tub underneath, and took a gun loaded with a bullet, held it underneath,

keg and let down the contents into the tub. The Pocket vs. The Heart. þÿ We mentioned sometime since, that Margaret Dinsmore, a very pretty girl, had brought an action for " breach of promise," against Andrix A. Foster, a very handsome young man, and recovered fifty dollars damages, in the Common Pleas Court. The general impression, at the time, was that the Jury could not have thought the gentleman worth much, or they would not have rated him at a price which was pronounced as cheap as Albany beef. þÿ It seems, however, that Margaret, the dear good soul, set a higher value on him than the Jury aforesaid. She knew his value well. þÿ They had walked together, and gone to lecture together, and sang out of the same hymn book together, and sat up and chatted by the same fire together, until it began to strike little ones, and was time to gather the ashes together, and say "good night" together. To her, Andrix was a pearl of price þÿ not to be cast away as the plaything and gewgaw of a few hours of idleness, to fall on the stream of time and float down with its myriads of feathcrless bipeds, to the ocean of oblivion where " there is no delight in men," þÿ nor women either. Andrix had been to her as a jaspar or sardonyx stone, set in fine gold, and worn "as a frontlet before her eyes." Fifty dollars was no price at all for such a jewel. A thousand would hardly begin to be, and Margaret determined to have the opinion of the Supreme Court, and presented herself before J udge Shaw. After three days of trial, the Chief Justice summed up the evidence,

with his accustomed perspicuity, and left the þÿ decision to the Jury. They decided that Andrix was worth two hundred and fifty dollars, and directed that sum to be paid to Margaret accordingly. From the Barbados Mercury, March 5, IB,'Hi.) We experience a great gratification in being enabled, through the polite attention of a mercantile friend, to place before our readers the King's Speech, upon the opening of Parliament, on the 4th ultimo, a copy of which was received yesterday, by his Majesty's ship Vestal, twenty-four days from Spithead, and obligingly forwarded to this office, for insertion : " My Lords and Gentlemen, " It is with much satisfaction that I again meet the great Council of the Nation assembled in Parliament. I am ever anxious to avail myself of your advice and assistance, and I rejoice that the present state of public affairs, both at home and abroad, is such as to permit you to proceed without delay or interruption to the calm examination of these measures which will be submitted to your consideration. " 1 continue to receive from my Allies, and generally from all Foreign Powers, assurances of their unaltered desire to cultivate with me those friendly relations which it is equally my wish to maintain with them ; and the intimate union which happily subsists between this country and France, is a pledge to Europe for the continuance of the general peace. " Desirous on all occasions to use my friendly endeavours to remove causes of disagreement between other Powers, I have offered my mediation in order to compose the difference which has arisen between France and the United States. This ofTer has been accepted by the King of the French ; the answer of the President of the United States

has not yet been received ; but I entertain a confident hope that a misunderstanding between two nations so enlightened and highminded, will be settled in a manner satisfactory to the feelings and consistent with the honor of both. ' I have still to lament the continuance of the civil contest in the Northern Provinces of Spain. The measures which I have taken, and the engagements into which I have entered sufficiently prove my deep anxiety for its termination ; and the prudent and vigorous conduct of the present Government of Spain inspires me with the hope that the authority of the Queen will soon be established in every part of her dominions, and that the Spanish Nation, so long connected by friendship with Great Britain, will again enjoy the blessings of internal tranquillity and union. 1 have given directions that there shall be laid before you the treaty which 1 have concluded with the Queen of Spain for the suppression of the slave trade. " Gentlemen of the House of Commons, " 1 have directed the estimates of the year to be prepared and laid before you without delay. They have been framed with the strictest regard to a well-considered ceremony. Patterson, came up from Hampton Roads yesterday morning in tow of the steam boats 1'atiick Henry and Thomas Jefferson, and anchored off the Naval Hospital. The Delaware is a ' native' of this port þÿ Here it was that she was launched, and the stirring scene was witnessed by us and duly recorded in these columns. We have watched every movement of this gallant vessel since, and when we saw her well known person looming upon us as she pressed majestically onward, we hailed her as wc would a fellow citizen arrived after a long and dangerous voyage. When we saw her fairly come to anchor, and alone in her majesty, we could hardly laugh at the unconscious declaration of the Congressman, when he saw a 74 for the fist time þÿ 44 By jucks, we are a great nation, to be sure !"

The funeral of the daughter of Commodore Patterson took place yesterday. We regret to add that the extreme inclemency of the weather prevented that full exhibition of sympathy on the part of our citizens which was sensibly felt for the situation of a distinguished officer, whose first duty on touching his native earth after a long absence was to commit a beloved daughter to its bosom. þÿ JMiss Patterson, whose death on board the Delaware on Mondav night last we have already noticed, is represented to have been one of the most accomplished women of her day. She had travelled extensively in Europe, and observing the passing scenes with that exquisite delicacy which is peculiar to the cultivated intellect of woman, she rendered her conversation the delight of all her acquaintance. She had been indisposed for some time, and the late severe weather increased her calamity. Still the faint hope was cherished that her ej es might rest once more on her native land that she might even touch its soil þÿ but me fond hope, although it lingered a- while, was at last delusive. Her remains now repose in the new burying ground, and although in a land of strangers, there are those among us w ho knew her worth and will long cherish her memory. þÿ American Beacon, Feb. 20,

MR. E. L. BULWER. The most distinguished literary man in the House is Mr. E. L. Bulwer, Member for Lincoln, and author of Pelliam Eugene Aram, <$c. He does not speak often. When lie does, his speeches arc not only previously turned over with great care in his mind, but are written out at full length, and committed as cureiuily to memory as if fie were going to recite them at some annual examination of some public school. He is artificial throughout þÿ the mere creatine of sell discipline þÿ in all his exhibitions in the House. You see art and ullectation in his very personal appearance in fiis mode of diessing, and in his every moment. Une of his schoolfellows has told me, that at school, he was as much noted tor his attention to the cut of his coat as to his intchccluui pursuits. 11c is the same man still. He is a great patron of the tailor and perrug uier. þÿ He is always dressed in the exticmc of fashion. He some times eliects a modesty of demeanour ; but it is too transparent to deceive any one who has the least discernment. \ ou see at once that he is on stiiis; and it cost him an effort even to assume the virtue which he has not. His mariner of speaking is very affected þÿ the management of his voice is especially so ; but for this he would be a pleasant speaker. His voice though weak is agreeuble, and he speaks with considerable fluency. His speeches are usually argumentative. Y'ou see at once that he is a person of great intellectual acquirements, though his speeches appear

much better in print than when you hear thorn delivered. His articulation is impaired by the aflected manner of his pronunciation and the rapidity of his utterance. His favouiite subject in the house is the repeal of the taxes of newspapers. On that question he makes a motion every session. I believe him to be sincerely anxious for the abolition of those duties : but had he, last year, not yielded to the previously-expressed solicitations of the friends of Mr. Spring Rice to withdraw his motion, the newspaper taxes would by this time have ceased to exist. There were a considerable majority in the house at the time

in favour of this motion ; and I recollect observing the exultation expressed in their countenances at their anticipated triumph. But the secret of the matter was, that he brought forward his motion at that time, not with the intention of carrying it, but for the mere sake of a little display, coupled, perhaps, with a wish to make an appearance of redeeming a pledge he had previously given to bring the subject forward in the course of the session. Mr Bulwer is a fine-looking man. He is rather tall and handsome. His complexion is fair, and his hair of a dark-brown. His nose is aquiline and prominent, and his face angular. He usually wears a green surtout ; he is young 1 cannot give his precise age, but 1 am certain that it cannot exceed thirty-five. He is understood to average from £1200 to £1500 a year by his literary labours.

IlYGKIANISM. (From the London Atlas, January, 24, 1836.) The Following communication from Dr. Lynch will he perused with much satisfaction by all those who are friendly to the cause of Hygeianism. Dr. Lynch, with a manly and noble feeling, declares to the world that he has changed his tenets, and become a staunch believer in our doctrine. He need not apprehend any charge being made of inconsistency. Mutability is one of the most distinguished characters of the human mind, and a man can only be praised for relinquishing errors he had imbibed, and embracing a doctrine which he had doubted, but on the truth of which he now places implicit faith. We sincerely congratulate our Hygeian þÿ friends of brilliant success attending upon the proon the accession of strength we shall acquire in consequence of Dr. Lynch becoming an adherent to þÿHvgeianism. This gentleman is well known in London as a physician of great talent; and last year his lectures at the Theatre of Medicine in Webb street, Borough. þÿ On Morbid þÿAnatomy, were remarked by the numerous auditors who attended as being replete with profound science and interesting research. COPY. London, 12th January, 1830. Sir To a mind properly constituted, they þÿ can be no greater satisfaction than affording to our suffering fellow creatures ready and certain relief. For the purpose of affording such was medicine studied, and medical laws established in order to secure the better regulation of its members, whose modern improvements in science have tended, it has been announced, to the rendering medicine a study of more

decided philosophic induction than hitherto ; at the same time it cannot be denied that it has cast a "nil of mystery over that which ought to be simplified However, those boasted strides in science, and the march of intellect are rapidly leading the nations of the earth to embrace and follow that true and scientific light which has nature for its instructor, and reason and experience for its guides, backed by the soundest philosophy, which will guide them into temple the of health and felicity. As it is the duty of every man to know himself physically as well as morally, imposin' on us as a due sense of the importance of becoming acquainted with the simplest laws of health, induced me to inquire into, and study attentively, the Hygeian theory and treatment of disease, viz. þÿ that all diseases to which the human frame is subject arise trom impurity of the blood and fluids, and that purgation, and consequent purification, was to be rendered effective in the cure of all maladies. The numberless records of cures laid before me, and the cases I have both seen and had under my care, have established a conviction firm and unshaken as to its superior excellency, determining me on no longer adhering to the trammels of system and the rules of profession. but at once adopt and practise that theory which should add to my pathological information the simplest remedial knowledge. According to the plan which 1 have laid down for mv guidance, it would seem necessary that I should anticipate the severity of
criticism, by an elaborate justification of the criminality my apparent presumption of in throwing off the mystic forms which encircle the medical graduate, and which is inspired

To apologize, indeed, for efforts which originate in the simple and natural wish to become a fellow labourer in the grandest of all works, doiug good, implies, at first sight, a superfluous degree of modesty ; yet, when we consider the vast and formidable host of medical aspirants, who profess the same laudable motive, our surprise at this timidity vanishes, belore the still greater temerity, which urges a fresh candidate to bespeak the interest ol an experienced and enlightened public.
