An honest sailor who had lately returned from an successful voyage, was determined to see every diversion which was going on in London at that time of the year. Accordingly he went to see a play, or rather a farce, at Bartholomew Fair. Every thing was con-' ducted to the satisfaction of such an audience and received with much mirth to the end of the second act ; when the benches of the gallery on which the sailor was placed, being overloaded, suddenly broke down with a dreadful crash and a horrible outcry ; many of the company being much hurt, and one or two having their arms or legs broken. The sailor, however, not having suffered by his fall, clapped his oaken þÿstaff under his arm, sacked up liis trousers and walked off, so þÿw cll satisfied With his entertainment, that the next night he came again to the theatre with great punctuality, and seated himself in the very same place as on the preceding night. The same farce was repeated ; and at the end of the second act, our sailor with great fortitude composes himself, and calls out to those who sat next him þÿ Come, my master, now for it ; we are just a going ! Sit fast my lads þÿ! þÿ In reality, the honest tar considered the falling of the gallery, though a very tragical event, as the principal part of the entertainment, for which he had paid his sixpence. þÿ Leigh Hunt's London Journal.

A Quaker Woman's Sermon. þÿ Dear Friends þÿ There are three things 1 very much wonder at : þÿ The first is, that children should be so foolish as to throw up stones, brickbats, and dubs into fruit trees to knock down the fruit; if they would let it alone, it would fall itself. The second is, that men should be so foolish and even so wicked as to go to war and kill one another; if they would only let one another alone, they would die of themselves. And the third and last thing, which I wonder at, is, that young men should be so unwise as to go after the young women ; if they would only stay at home, the young women would come after them.

Constantinople, Nov. 25. þÿ A Creek is now hanging up in Constantinople at the door of a Turkish lady, and lie came there in the fol- 'owing manner þÿ He was by trade a tailor, ami used to sit industriously at his little open shop nearly opposite the house of the lady in question, who for hours together was wont to feast her eyes on the handsome young giaour, as she peeped through her small cagevvork jealousy. Her breast was inflamed with love; and as a Turkish lady in such case docs not Let concealment, liUe a worm l1 tlie buJ, Feed on her damask chekv they soon eame to a good understanding. þÿ Their meetings at first were well arranged, and there was little danger of a discovery, and thus nearly two years ran on smoothly. þÿ Constant success led, as usual, to carelessness, and finally the tailor was caught in the arms of his mistress He was soon dragged before the Seraskier, and the evidence being conclusive, he was condemned to the penalty he could not but be aware would follow the discovery. The law of the land condemns to death such intercourse between a Turkish woman and an infidel man. The lady, however, has been allowed to live for the present, as she is in the way that ' women wish to be who love their" þÿ tailors ! It is very possible she may escape, though now confined, until she shall be " confined," in order that afterwards she may make the acquaintance of the Bosphorus sewed up in a bag. The hanging ot the Greek has created a great sensation here, as such severity is extremely rare in the

present day. For one life now sacrificed to maintain the law in this country, J should say twenty at least are sacrificed in England. þÿ Herald Correspondence. 0 0 Statesmanlike Relaxation. þÿ It may not be unsatisfactory to such as admire splendid talents, like those displayed by Mr. Pitt, to have an instance given now his great mind could amuse itself by jocularity. As 1 was one day passing through the rooms after my accustomed avocations, I met with Mr. Pitt and Lady Charlotte Gordon conversing together in the drawing-room. Lady Charlotte having some order to give me, commenced as usual, " Mr. D'Amour" Mr. Pitt purposely interrupting speech by her taking the sentence from her lips, added, " You arc desired to bring one of the Shetland ponies up stairs immediately." I smiled, and bowed acquiescence ; but stood a moment or two, to give the lady time to finish what she intended to have said. What Mr. Pitt had proposed, however, jest, she determined to surprise is him with in earnest; and while they were mutually laughing, she stepped towards me, and in a low tone of voice, bade me do as he had said. I hastened down stairs, being always well pleased to fulfil a good-humoured command, sought the groom, got the pony saddled, and had him led up stairs; the easy ascent of which he mounted very gracefully. When I opened the door and announced the arrival, (and surely it was the first announcement of the kind ever made,) Mr. Pitt's powerful voice, exercised in abundant laughter,

resounded through a great part of the mansion. After parading the pony round, the Prime Minister, to finish the joke, tied a white handkerchief to the bit of the bridle, and led him down stairs with his own hand, þÿ not, however, till the animal had deposited upon the floor of the drawing-room an indubitable proof of his having made himself quite at home þÿ a revolving and unknown cause, fly over Memoirs of Air. 3ia&23'Jl2IfB3 A'TtS. Irish Emigrants in America. þÿ Here comes a ship load of Irish. They land upon the wharfs of New York in rags and open kneed breeches, with their raw looks and bare necks. They flourish their cudgels, throw up their torn luits, and cry " Hurrah lor General Jackson 1" They get drunk and kick up a row þÿ lend their forces to any passing disturbance, and make an early acquaintance with the inferior of the lock ups. From New York they go in swarms to the canals, rail roads, and public works, where they perform the labour which the Americans are not inclined to do. Now and then they get up a fight among themselves in the style of the ould Ireland, and perhaps kill one another, expressing great indignation and surprise when they find they must ansvvei for it, though they arc in a free country. By degrees, the more thirfty get and keep money, and, diving deeper into the Continent, purchase lands ; while the intemperate and irreclaimable vanish from the surface. The Americans complain and justly, of the disorderly population which Ireland throws into the bosom of the Union, but there are many reasons why they should be borne with. They, with the poor Germans, do the work which Though the fathers may he irreclaimable, the children become good citizens, and there is no finer race in the world, both for powers of mind and body, than the Irish, when favoured by education, and under proper controul. In one thing the emigrant Irish of every class distinguish themselves above the people of

other nations, and this is in the love and kind, ly feeling which they cherish towards their native land, and towards those whom they have left behind ; a fact proved by the large sums which are yearly transmitted from thcin to the mother country, in aid of their poverty stricken relatives, Latrobe's Rambler in þÿ JAortJi America.

A Leech Burrowing in the Human Thigh. þÿ Dr. Roe, of Cavan, mentioned a curious case of this nature at the Dublin meeting. þÿ He said that he was called some time back to visit the daughter of a farmer residing at Drum, in the county of Cavan ; the girl Lad been attacked several days previous witli inilamation of the thigh, and at the time of his arrival was labouring under severe symptomic fever, with delirium. The thigh was tense, red, and shining, enlarged to nearly twice the natural size, and very painful. No cause could be assigned for the disease, and he was informed that, until the time of the present attack, she had always enjoyed excellent health. Having ascertained the existance of a collection of matter under the fascia, he made an incision, &evacuated abowlful of pus, mixed with what he considered to be clots of blood. His attention was not directed to the contents at that time ; besides the room was dark and he was anxious to give vent to the pus as quickly as possible, as the patient was extremely restless. On emptying the matter from the bowl on a clean flag outside the door the þÿgirl mother s was surprised to find amongst it a leech, coiled up, quite alive, and moving actively. She immediately brought the leech to him, and it continued to live for several days afterwards. Oft inquiring minutely into the history of the case, he found that some days before she first complained of the limb, she had been gathering water cresses in a ditch ; and had felt hurt in or about the ancle

of the inflamed limb, but did not pay much attention to it at the time. On examining the ancle he found a triangular cicatrix such as that which might be produced by a lecch-bitc. This fact would seem to prove that such animals can enter, burrow in, and preserve their vitality in the soft parts of the human body. A member asked whether Dr. Roe meant to state that the leech had entered in the manner supposed ? Dr. Roe stated that he did not know any other way in which it could enter. The animal in question was called a horse leech, and which is generally found in ditches and standing pools. þÿ Medical Cazclte.

Death of a Miser. þÿ A few days ago an old miser, named Webb, who has for several years resided in an obscure lodging in Barrack-court, Woolwich, called upon a Mr. White, a broker, residing in Powis street, in the same parish, to inquire whether he would allow him to lodge with him, as he lmd been uncomfortable for some time past. The request was complied with, and in the evening he took possession of his new apartments. He had not retired to rest but a very short time before he was taken ill, and at his request two medical men were sent for. Upon the arrival of Messrs þÿM Donald and Gaut they pronounced him to be in a dying state, which was no sooner communicated to tfie patient than he ordered an attorney to he sent for, as he wished to make his will. An attorney was speedily in attendance. The old man, raising himself up in bed, bequeathed to his daughter £ 100; to three nephews, £3(1, £40, and £50 each. Upon being asked if he had a wife, he replied, þÿ Yes ; but he had been parted from her three times; that she had been in a workhouse near .Stroud, in Kent, for a number of years, and that he did not intend to leave her a single penny, as she was very comfortable. He had also two brothers and another daughter, who had all behaved ill

towards him, and ho would leave them nothing. Upon being asked to whom he lolt the residue of his property, lie replied to Mr. White, for his kindness ; at the same handing the attorney a paper, which upon being opened was found to contain securcties for upwards of £ 800 in the Bank of England ; so that Mr. White (who is sole executor) will, after paying the respective legacies, clear upwards of £ 500 by his lodger, who continued to get w'orse and died on Sunday. It is a remarkable fact that the deceased (who was 75 years of age) has been frequently seen to pick up bones and rags in the street, and put them into his pocket ; and at the same time of his death he was in a most tiltiiy condition. þÿ Morning Herald.

CAPTAIN BACK. This gallant and enterprising officer arrived at Liverpool a lew days ago, and has since been presented to his Majesty. The Alhenatum gives the following outline of his proceedings : þÿ þÿ On the 7th June, 1834, he left Fort Reliance witlt his party, and was employed, during the remainder of that month, in transporting his boat and stores on rollers to his destined point of embarkation on the Thleweecho dezeth, þÿ a very arduous service, the distance being above 200 miles, and his people being in far from vigorous condition, in consequence of the spare diet to w hich they had been subjected during the previous winter. The task was, however, successfully accomplished, and on the 7th July, the party consisting of Captain Back, Mr. King, his surgeon and only assistant, and eight men all Europeans, bade adieu to their companions, and proceeded down the river in the direction ascertained the previous season. The stream was at first deep, and interrupted by rapids as it cut its way transversely through a mountain range running East and West ; but beyond this it proceeded to the northward, with little interruption, till in latitude 65 deg. 40 min. N., longitude 106 deg. 35 min. W., it took a sudden turn to the East, thereby destroying the hopes up to this time entertained, of its entering the sea near Bathurst's Inlet. It now became very broad, and broken, as it were, into a succession of small lakes, terminating in one so large that it showed a clear horizon on several points of the compass ; and here the

expedition was much embarrassed by ice, so that, for above twenty miles, it was only enabled to advance by severe exertion. þÿ On recovering the clear water ; however, the stream speedily again contracted, still trending easterly, and even S. E. and much broken by rapids and cascades, until at þÿ length, in latitude 65 deg. 54 min. N., longitude 98 deg. 10 min. W , (not far, thercfere from the head of Wager Bay,) it bursts with great fury between four granite mountains, and flowed thence tolerably directly towards the North. It also here became again very wide þÿ from half a mile to a mile þÿ and was even more broken with rapids and whirlpools than before ; the adjoining country being in like manner rugged and hilly. The first Esquimaux were met not far from the sea, fishing at the foot of a considerable fall ; and though they seemed in the beginning disposed to be hostile, they became afterwards very obliging and serviceable. On the 29th July the expidition reached the sea in latitude 67 deg. 7 min, N., longitude 94 deg. 40 min. W. þÿ The river first terminated in a narrow estuary, much embarrassed by shoals and sand banks ; and the view to the North was in some measure closed in by a lofty headland, belonging to the eastern mountains, (afterwards called Victoria headland.) The opposite shores, however, speedily increased their distance from each other ; that to the westward falling back in a direction nearly N. W., while that to the eastward trended off to N. E. | E. : þÿ and as Captain Back

was now to the eastward of Captain James þÿRoss P s illar, he considered it to be his duty to proceed to the westward, and so endeavour to approach it. But the drift ice was so closely packed on the shore in this direction, and was at the same time so fre

N., long. 96 deg. 22 min W., when it bore about N. W. by N., distant eighty three þÿmiles. From this point a clear icy horizon was seen in the N. N. W., in about which direction there seemed no doubt that there was a passage to the open sea, the tides coming up from this quarter, and the verrebrm of a whale being round driven on the coast opposite to it, with several pieces of drift wood, little sudden with water, and of a kind (the white pine) known to be peculiar to the banks of þÿM Kenzie River. Due North were two blue objects, which seemed to be large islands In the S. E. were water and ice, with what is denominated a water sky beyond them. þÿ them In the East the sea was clear, with one small island bearing E. by S., from fifteen to twenty miles distant ; and to the right of this w as also a wide open space before coming to the eastern land. þÿ The packed ice seemed chiefly confined to the western shore : and beyond it especially to the eastward, the passage appeared quite free. Had Captain Back not known, therefore, of Captain þÿRoss sreturn, he would have proceeded in that direction ; and so, probably, have set at rest a question w hich he has now rather raised them decided, viz , whether Captain Ross was not merely on an island, and never on the mainland of America at all. Under his circumstances, however, and with the extremely severe task before

him of re-ascending so rapid and broken a river as the Thleweecho to his winter quarters, he would have been inexcusable had he quitted the coast in his solitary, and by this time also damaged, boat Accordingly, he set out on his return on the 15th of August, having previously obtained from his friendly Esquimaux a delineation, after their manner, of the adjoining coast, which he has brought home w ith him, and which, so far as he went, was remarkably corroborated by the results of his own survey. He also ascended the most favourably placed of the neighbouring hills, so as to extend his sphere of vision; and thus took every step possible, in his circumstances, to render the results of his journey satisfactory. In ascending the river on his return he was obliged to abandon his boat, and proceed on foot over the young ice ; but his people, being well supplied with provisions, did not suffer materially under this additional fatigue. They arrived at Fort Reliance on the 27 th of September, after an absence of three months and a half on their arduous service ; and may all be expected in England, at the latest, by the þÿHudson Bay s þÿCompany ship s in November. Their gallant leader has been enabled to precede them by returning through Canada. þÿ With regard to the results of his journey, it is difficult, as yet, to speak positively, with only a meagre outline of his proceedings before us, as contained in his letters, and without the detail which, in such subjects, is indispensable towards the formation of a

matured opinion. Yet, on the face of his narrative, great dangers and difficulties appear to have been boldly and ably surmounted : while these have led him across a considerable extent (almost 1,000 miles) of entirely new ground, of which we had no previous knowledge, unless through India report, now indubitably proved, in the main, incorrect. But beyond this, the results of his labours arc also extensively negative. þÿ

Our previous conceptions of the configuration of the north-eastern extermity of America, especially as founded on Sir John R<r ' representations, are much modified by thAn , and, individually, we now believe that h' Boothia was merely an island, none of his statements being irreconcileable with this hypothesis, except the difference of level which he alleges that he found between the seas on either side of its peninsula. We cannot help hoping, however, that the real fact may yet speedily, as it may certainly now easily, be ascertaided. Besides what Captain þÿBack s details, when obtained, may do towards settling the question, nothing seems more certain, from the result of both these last expeditions þÿ(Ross and s þÿBack s,) than that the ground respectively examined by may easily be gone over again þÿ From Chesterfield or Wager Inlets, the distance to the Thleweecho is now shown to be short ; while that from Repulse Bay to the sea, into which it falls, is probably still shorter. An expedition, wintering at any of these points, with the means of constructing boats, in preparation for the following season, could easily, cheaply, and certainly complete the bottom of Regent's Inlet ; while one or two vessels, either sent down the Inlet or to the westward of Boothia, as might be thought best, could complete the observations about the magnetic pole, begun by Captain James lloss, and probably connect his farthest with Cape Turnagain also, in one or two seasons. Mo value need be attached to the bringing

these vessels back ; if they got hampered, they might be abandoned, and the crews return in iheir boats, as Captain Ross did, to a fixed rendezvous in Lancaster Sound or Repulse Bay. Surely an object which has been so long pursued has from that circumstance alone, acquired sufficient value to warrant another trial like this ; and we know that neither are the old Artetic hands worn out, nor would new volunteers be wanting, who would desire nothing so much as to be sent on such a service. At this very moment, also, it is understood that the Board of Admiralty contemplates instituting a series of magnetical observations in the southern hemisphere ; and honour, if not even possibly scientific advantage, would be acquired by the simultaneous pursuit of a similar series in the opposite þÿquarter.

Our friends (and, by our friends we mean those who subscribe to our paper and pay their subscription,) are for the most part annoyed by a tribe who, according to the class of Natural History in which the West Indian Editors have ranked them, are termed þÿ þÿborrowers. To such an extent of evil have t lie propensities of this tribe proceeded, without restraint, that the newspaper press here is threatened with almost certain annihilation, since, in a short lime, one newsprper will be made to serve a hundred readers, at the expense of the goodnatured but honorable man who thinks the editor or the printer, like every honest laborer, worthy of his hire. We cannot imagine any thing more contemptible in the character of a man than imposing, on the generosity of his neighbor to obtain that for which he ought to pay himself. As Johnson said of pun-makers, we will imitate with regard to borrowers: þÿ He who being able to subscribe to a paper, and does not, but sends to his neighbor to borrow, will not hesitate to pick a pocket ! Subscribers! file your papers, and at the end of the year have the volumes bound, if you think the papers worth it. You will then have the best excuse for refusing your sponging neighbors, the favor which, much to your annoyance, is twice a week applied for, as a worn out and tattered paper can be in such case of no use to you. In making these remarks we shall offend no subscriber þÿ each one must agree with us in our remarks þÿ and once, at all events

we beg that this paper may be lent out, and if at any time a future number be applied for þÿ for þÿHeaven s sake put down the applicant as an incorrigible vagabond. We beg leave to draw the very serious attention of our friends and subscribers to the above sensible þÿremarks! Es. R. A<

.' Jl WATl 4 -SU#«4. r J ft I E TIE S. PARENTAL INDULGENCE. The following extract on the efl'ects of parental indulgence, we think just and forcible. There can be no real excellence of character without a capacity for self-denial. We must be able to prefer the interest and pleasure of others to what man be more strictly styled our own, or we can have no happy experience of social life. The true office of a great mind is to prefer and indulge others where it may be done without injury, and to restrain and control them, when he may, to their profit. This is self-government. This is action with a reason, and on a principle that seeks first the good of others, and then its own reward in that good But there are some minds so truly enslaved, that they never feel important except when they are indulged. In their estimation, to be denied any gratification is to be wronged. They could be borne, perhaps, if you could always please them witli indulgence, but they take every thing so much as their due, that they never feel obligation for kindness, and it can seldom be so exact and seasonable but they will be impatient with it. These are those troublesome people that have in early life always had their own way. þÿ It is notorious that indulged children become hard-hearted, ungrateful, cruel to their parents in advanced life. There is no true and abiding love towards a parent, where there is not genuine respect for authority. They first contemn his authority, then despise him, then hate him, then resent, disregard and abuse

him. They claim it as a right to have their wishes gratified ; they revenge refusal. Why should they not ? They are but carrying out the principles in which he has educated them. The parent has taught them so. He has not trained them up in the way they should go, but in the way they would go. He has suffered human wisdom to reverse the mandate of divine. He has accommodated his government to their selfish wills, instead of subduing those wills to rightful authority. The consequence is, a continued and growing misunderstanding and variance between them and thfeir parents, then between them and their Bible, then between them and their God, and this breach gradually widens to an impassable þÿgulf. More persons probably are injured by indulgence than by neglect. Neglect diives them upon their own resources, opens their eyes to reality, to themselves as they are and may be; to the world as it is and will be. They now do for themselves what others could not do for them. They begin to take the storms as the oak does, without dismay or harm. Others have been so much loved, and so tenderly treated that, like plants which have grown in the shade, they cannot bear the sun which brings forward and ripens all others of their kind. They are indeed so sensitive, and take every little disappointment so hard, that one must live solely to invent their enjoyment, and to watch and anticipate their wants, or they will be likely to become disaffected with life, and with all around them. Parents should love their children mor« after

the manner of the love of God to them, with too much benevolence and sagacity to indulge in the selfishness which too often prevents proper discipline, and "with too much regard for the purity and simplicity of childhood, to be in any degree a party to impairing them, by undue indulgence. þÿ American Paper.

For the great inconvenience of a bald rate, our ancestors found a very simple remedy ; it consists of garden snails, taken from their shells, and pounded together with horseleeches, bees, wasps, and some salt. These ingredients were mixed up, put into a hot lied for eight days, and then smeared over the bald head, on which they soon brought an ample harvest of hair. When the reverse of this process was required, as in tire case of a lady whose hair grew too long on her tiers, the rebel growth was soon dispersed bv the application of the following lotion : þÿ Take twenty green frogs and a pint of wine, put. both into a pot, which keep forty days in the sun; the residue is the lotion. þÿ The Doctor

By the latest arrivals from Paris we learn that the American question is creating a much deeper interest in the minds of the Paris Politicians than it originally did. The Warlike preparations at the ports of Toulon and Brest, together with the accounts received from America of the temper and disposition of Mr. President Jackson towards the government of France, have given rise to serious apprehensions in the minds of many that the present dispute will not be accommodated but that a rupture between France and the United States is daily becoming more probable. The question will not remain long doubtful. The message of the President to Congress will probably determine the point of peace or war between the two countries. The time fixed for the meeting of the French Chambers has been again altered. þÿ The 29th of December is the day now named as that on which they are to assemble. Their meeting is thus accelerated by at least a fortnight. No reason is assigned for this change, but the public supply one by imputing it to the apprehension entertained by the government of an unfavourable determination of the existing differences between the two countries. þÿ Watchman, Nov. 25.

The trial of Fieschi and his accomplices is fixed to take place before the Courts of Peers about the middle of December, so that it may conclude previously to the meeting of the Chambers. Late accounts from Algiers anþÿnp nce t he arrival of the Duke of Orleans at that plaee on the 10th instant. He was to quit Algiers for Oran on the 15th. The intelligence from Spain contained in the Paris papers furnishes us with nothing of importance which we have not already given. Conjectures on the contents of the speech to be delivered by the Queen at the opening of the Chambers from the principal feature ; they are various, and receive their colouring from the wishes and political bias of those from whom they emanuate.

FRANCE. The differences wi ll the United States appear to be seriously viewed by the French press. The Constitutionel publishes a correspondence from New York of the 15th of Nov., which represents public opinion as most averse to the concession of any explanation, and the American naval officers as loudly urging an expedition for levying a contribution of 25,000,000f. on the French West Indian Islands, and Gen. Jackson has determined not to utter one word of conciliation as long as he shall remain in office, Both the Constitutionel and the Courier Francois affirm that several ships of war are being fitted out in great haste at Brest and Toulon, which under command of Admiral de Mackau, are to proceed to the West India station in order to protect french commerce from aggression. þÿ The Dehats observes that the recall of Mr. Barton might have been anticipated from the personal dispositions of General Jackson; but that although it is difficult to foresee to what extremities the President may suffer himself to be led, it believes that no rupture is to be apprehended. and that Congress will not sanction the adoption of any \iolent or decisive measures. From þÿ the Watchman. Nov 25.

It is stated in the Journal of Mexico of the 3rd of September, that an action had taken place at sea between the Montezuma schooner belonging to the Mexican republic, with a crew of fifty men and four guns, and the American schooner Ingham, likewise of four guns, but with a crew of 24 men. In consequence of this action, the American Schooner, after a dreadful combat, was obliged to run ashore. This battle, which was commenced by the American vessel, is generally considered as a provocation to war on the part of that nation. þÿ tit. James's Chronicle, Nov. 26.

Mr. Villiers has had several conferences with Senior Mendizabal, relative to a commercial treaty between England and Spain ; and the basis is now, for the first time, laid for ensuring advantages to the commerce of Great Britain, upon the system of reciprocity with regard to that of Spain. This has been the object of Mr. þÿVillier e s fforts with all former Administrations 1 but until the arrival of Senior Mendizabal at the head of affairs, there have always been obstacles which could not be surmounted. The basis having now been laid down þÿ the principle of untrainmelling commerce having been established þÿ Mr. Villiers prudently abstains from pressing the matter further upon Senior Mendizabal just now, because the latter is fully occupied in measures preparatory to the fast approaching meeting ol the Cortes ; in organising plans connected with the new levies, and other matters which will tend to the consolidation of public credit ; and thus the hands of Government having become strenghtened, and the wisdom of its course being displayed by the success of its measures, additional weight will be given to whatever decision may become to regarding a commercial treaty with Great Britain þÿ Ministerial Faper.

(From the Barbados Mercury, Jan. 5, 1830.) PROSPECTS OF WAR. The politicial aspects of Europe are commencing to occupy much more attention in the public mind, than they have lately done, and an impression has prevailed here that, in addition to the supposed disputes between the Courts of Paris and St. Petersburg, matters have not lately run so smooth between those of St Petersburg and Great B ritain, whilst it has even been confidently advanced that a correspondence has taken place between Lords Palmerston and Durham, relative to the necessity of demanding an explanation of the reply of the Czar to the address of the Deputies of Warsaw. If this is the case, the knell of departed Polish liberty has at last penetrated the dull aural functions of our protocolling Foreign Secretary and his colleagues, and, after the eleventh hour has passed away, perhaps has stimulated them to a feeble and useless remonstrance with the Northern Autocrat. Anticipations are also rife relative to the dispute between the French and United States Governments ; and parties who maintain that it is unavoidable, refer to the naval armaments fitting out at Brest and Toulon, whilst others as strenuously apply the cause of those naval preparations only to the anticipated desagremens between France and Russia. A good deal of anxiety prevails for the arrival of the inaugural address of the Queen- Regent of Spain to the Cortes, as it is anticipated that the contents of that now important speech will fully disclose the policy, foreign and domestic, of that Government.

Our statement that a British man of war would proceed to Barcelona with arms and ammunition has been confirmed by the fact of the Rodney, 92 guns, being ordered round from Portsmouth to Plymouth for that purpose. þÿ Herald, Nov. 21.

Considerable sensation continues to be created by the departure of the American Charge <L Affaires from Paris ; but in the present state of the dispute between France and the United States, it is difficult to form an idea of the manner in whicli it will terminate. The American Government is clearly right in principle, and if it acts with a tithe of the energy which it displayed in the discussion of the question of the French claims, there seems no reason to doubt that a hostile collision will be the consequence. In the prospect of reprisals on the French trade being attempted, the French Government has already ordered two ships of the line to proceed to the West Indies, and a .squadron to cruise ofT the Beleario Islands ; and should the opposing parties meet, as most likely they will, a trifle only will be required to kindle the spark of contention into a flutne. þÿ Glasgow Courier, IV ov. 17.

The Courier Francais has the þÿfollowing: "A Toulon journal has given a series of articles, maintaining that the American navy must have the advantage over the French in actions of ship with ship, and stating that the navy of the United States is at present composed of seven ships of the line of 74 guns, one of which is arined and equipped,

This makes a total of 35 ships ; but we have reason to believe that this account is incorrect, and that at this moment the United States have 00 ships of different rates, either at sea or in port. Intoxicating Powers of different Liquors. Professor Beck, of New York, undertook a series experiment upon wines at the request of of some Temperance Societies. The results agree generally with those of Brandy, published 20 years ago. The alcohol or spirit existing in wine is not combined witn the vegetable infusion, but merely mixed with it. The union, however, grows more perfect as the wine gets older, and hence old wines are less intoxicating than new. Supposing the por lion of alcohol in wine, to be the measure of its effects on the brain, the following table (the fractions rejected) is given by Mr. Beck as representing the intoxicating power of dilabout the common strength is taken as a standard þÿ: Brandy, 100; strongest Medetra, 48 ; weakest Madeira, 36 ; Port (average), 42 ; Bucellas, 35 ; Sherry, 33: Torres Vedras, 38; Aauterne, 24 ; Claret (average), 21 ; American wine, 21 : metheglin, 20; ale 20; beer, 14; cider (average), 9. It will be observed that a bottle of the strongest Madeira is neaily equal to half a bottle brandy ; ol and a bottle of average Port rather exceeds two fifths of a bottle of brandy. WlI.mam IV. at Gibraltar in 1781. It was in Admiral Rodney's fleet that our present gracious Sovereign (then Prince William Henry) visited Gibraltar, and in contributing to its relief made his first appearance as a defender of that throne which it has pleased Providence to permit his Majesty to adorn. His Royal Highness served as a midshipman under Admiral Digby, in the Prince George, and on one occasion in particular a circumstance occurred which Englishmen may well be proud of. The Spanish Admiral Don Juan Langara (then a prisoner on Board the British fleet,) visiting Admiral Digby one morning, was of course introduced to his Royal Highness. During the conference between the Admirals, Prince William Henry withdrew, and when it was intimated that Don Juan wished to retire, his Royal Highness appeared as the midshipman on duty, and respectfully informed the Admiral that the boat was manned. The Spaniard could not contemplate the son of England's Monarch acting as a petty officer unmoved, and turning to Admiral Digby and his suite, he exclaimed,. " Well does Great Britain merit the empire of the sea, when the humblest stations in her navy are supported by princes of the blood. þÿ Martin's History of the British Colonies.

Love in a chest. þÿ One of the strangest examinations ever heard of, took place at the Town Clerk's office in this city, on Saturday last. Benjamin Curtis is a servant of Mr. Heanley, of Branston Fen, and had formerly been fellow-servants with a young female, who, it seems, had become strongly attached to him. During the last week, the girl was observed lingering about Mr. Heanley's premises, snd some suspicions as to the nature of her connexion with Curtis were awakened. At length a female servant of Mr. Heanley found lier one day under Curtis's bed ; the strange girl, however, hid herself, and could not be found, on other residents of the house being fetched up stairs. No further discovery was made until Friday last, when a rumble being heard in Curtis's bedchamber, Mr. Heanley ran up stairs, but could see nothing, nor obtain any answer to his calls. The same noise being renewed ere Mr. Heanley reached the bottom ol the stairs, he again ascended, and seeing a chest move, he laid his hand on it, and knocked, and was answered by a low moan. Curtis was just at that moment returned from Lincoln, whither his master had dispatched him in the morning, on business. Mr. Heanley called him up stairs, and he immediately unlocked the chest, where lay the foolish but pitiable girl, half dead with suffocation ! Curtis immediately made confession that he had locked the girl up at her own request in the morning, on receiving his master's orders for Lincoln. She had been twelve hours crowded into a space

WE FREDERIK THE SIXTH, by the Grace of God, King of Denmark, the Vends and Goths, Duke of Slesvig, Holstein, Starmum, Ditmarsk, Luucnborg and Oldenburg, MAKE KNOYVN : That notwithstanding it had already been prescribed by an Ordinance respecting the Slave trade, given by our late lather of blessed memory, and dated on the 1 Oth ol March 1792, that all such trade was to cease trorn the year 1803 lor our royal subjects, as well on the coast of Africa, as in other places where it might exist, besides in Our Royal Colonies in the VVestindies, and that after the expiration of the said term, no male nor lctnale Negro should be allowed to be purchased by or for the Royal sybjects, nor to be shipped on board of vessels belonging to our Royal subjects, nor to be carried to the Royal Westindia Islands to be sold there, and that all trade contrary to this Law should Irom that time be considered as illegal, YVe have still, after having been invited by His Majesty the King of the French and His Alajesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, to join the conventions, which have been concluded by the said Powers under dates of the 30th of November 1831, and the 22nd of March 1833, for the suppression of the traffic in slaves, been willing to unite Our exertions with theirs, in order to take the most effectual means to suppress the said trade. In giving further publicity through this Our Ordinance to the said Conventions, to which we have

assented by a treaty of accession, signed by Us in our Royal Residence on the 2Uth of July 1834, as far as the rules and regulations therein laid down are hereafter to be observed by our trading and seafaring subjects, VVe have furtheimore resolved to prescribe such rules with regard to the mode of proceeding and judging of such cases, as might occur lrom the capture and delivery in our Ports of vessels, guilty or suspected of being engaged in the Slave trade, as would entirely secure Our own subjects and those of foreign powers, and to ordain those punishments, which will be inflicted in case of transgression of this Our Ordinance. YVe therefore make known and order as follows, viz : þÿ 1. In order to suppress by the most etTeetual means that nefarious traffic which is known under the name of the Slave trade, the contracting parties have agreed to grant unto each other a mutual right of search on board their merchant vessels for the discovery of such trade, but only within the waters hereafter described, viz : þÿ 1, Along the Western coast of Africa from Cape Verti to the distance of 10 degrees to the South of the Equator ; that is to say from the 10th degree of south latitude to the 15lh degree of north latitude, and as far us the 30th degree of West longitude, reckoning from the meridian of Paris. 2, All around the Island of Madagascar to the extent of about 20 leagues from that Island.

POST MORTEM EXAMINATIONS CORONER y JURIES and . Mr. Editor þÿ In the generality of those cases which appear to have passed a post mortem examination, it is stated in the reports ot the Inquests, that the parties died from inflammation of some part or parts of the Viscera ; and the case or cases previous to death having been in the hands of some one of the Faculty, Morison's Pills were generally resorted to, after the failure of other remedies- If these reports are to be depended upon, I think it would be highly proper that those medical men (who give their evidence before the Coroner) should state for public satisfaction what the case was, during their professional attendance upon the patients, and when Morison's Pills had been taken. Nothing can be more easy to state, upon the hypothesis of a careless and hasty post mortem examination than that " the parties died of inflammation, caused by taking Morison's Pills." Such a verdict must, I am sure, be considered by no means satisfactory, when it is remembered that those very morbid appearances which are generally described in the evidence might in all probability originate either from active or chronic inflammation of the mucus membranes of the intestines, colon or rectum, or constipation of the bowels, or general inflammation of the viscera requiring the nicest investigations apart from the action of any medicine, and admitting the patients were labouring under either of the above inflammations (in the event of blood letting and warm baths being omitted) there could be no

better practice than keeping the bowels in a state of solution, which I understand is the effect of Morison's Pills. It is generally said, a knowledge of disease is half the cure, and he who performs the best cure is the best physician ; now admitting the cause of death to some of those persons described as having died from having taken Morison's Pills, was inflammation of some particular parts of the intestines, attended more or less with constipation of the bow els ; under such circumstances, it is always a pleasing prognosis when the bowels slacken and answer the predication of the physician's prescription directed for that purpose (which is the first consideration of the practitioner, and to which his immediate attention is always called) ; I should therefore wish to be informed by those medical men who have figured at the late inquests, how aperients or purgatives in such cases could kill, even allowing for the idiosyncracy of tlie constitution. I know no more of the component part of Morison's Pills than I do of himself, for I know him not personally ; but 1 have often seen it stated in the public press that a portion of their composition consisted of gnmboge and aloes, upon which tlie stress ol poisoning is generally applied. This account of gamboge and aloes is fallacious, inasmuch as all antibilious and aperient pills generally consist in a composition of calomel, gamboge, scammony, aloes, jalap, die. &c well known to every branch of the faculty; therefore poisoning

upon this principle is totally out of the question. I often think when adverting to the stress laid upon the poisoning properties of gamhoge and aloes, what would he thought if an expoait ion were made of an absolute poison often introduced in pills under the hands of skilful physicians, such as the extract olafcrium, or croton oil, and very often the fluid rpueksiivor
>AST3x T$3tra»a>asK !Ra®aa»ast63 ATU3» J swallowed in large doses in cases of constipation of the bowels.

I can scarcely admit, after the long trial of the Hygeist's Pills by many thousand persons who have taken them to advantage, that they are deleterious. In illustration of this assertion, I shall quote the following circumstance which came under my own observation ! A clergyman of Cambridge, a gentleman of fortune and veracity, for some years was under my hands with all the threatened consequences attendant upon the derangement of the degestive functions ; the usual remedies prescribed in such cases, as well from other physicians as myself, proved abortive, and change of air and scene were resorted to instead of physic ; a few years ago he called upon me from Cambridge, and upon enquiry as to his health, he assured me he had been taking Morison's Pills with singular advantage and found himself considerably better ; that such was his faith in their curative qualities as to have induced him most strenuously to recommend them to a tradesman's wife of the town of Cambridge, as a last resort in a ease the faculty had given up; and 1 learnt afterwards in this case also Morison's Pills were beneficially employed. I)r. Nuttal, late physician to the Western General Dispensary, with whom I was upon terms of intimacy for 20 years, assured me he had a patient labouring under the most formidable symptoms of dyspepsia, and with whom he had tried all that human ingenuity could suggest in the science of physic ; one day when the patient informed him ol the distresses of his dreams & his eter-

nal headache, he very jocosely told him to try Morison's Pills ; the patient caught at the suggestion, and did so ; the doctor assured me upon his honour that the patient, in the course of six weeks, was most astonishingly better.

Nothing can be more easy than to raise a glare from post mortem examinations. I recollect being subpoenaed in Van Burchel's case at the Old Bailey, where he was arraigned upon the charge of murder, and in the evidence bv the surgeon who made the post mortem examination, he was accused of having perforated the rectum in passing a bougie in an old case, which put on the appearance of stricture or tumour in that part, and that the man died froin haemorrhage : þÿ so sure was the surgeon a conviction would follow, that he brought the rectum inflated into court, but from the extreme acuteness of an anatomical examination the surgeon was put under (by Mr. Broderick, the prisoner's counsel), the whole of the business cnited in a bottle of smoke, with a sensible rebuke from the learned judge (Hullock) who tried the ease, that it was extremely wrong to place a gentleman at the bar who endeavoured to do good to bis fellow-creatures ; at the same time the judge narrated a circumstance which occurred to himself in a remote part of the north of England, wherein ho was threatened with inflammation of the bowels, and no medical man residing within some miles, he sent for the farriei of the place, who administered a strong purgative, and the judge recovered. þÿ As his lordship justly observed, it would have been hard indeed that such a man should be prosecuted for practising without a license. From these facts, there appears sufficient reason to doubt the honesty of the evidence
given by the medical men upon coroner's juries, so far as poisoning resulting Ironi taking Morison's Pills is concerned.

I have no reason to espouse the cause of Mr. Morison or his Pills, but I am of opinion that their efficacy in their action upon the human frame has proved more beneficial than injurious; and although Mr. Morison may not be a medical man, that is not a justification for decrying his Pills, or for disparaging the man : such however, was the case with the immortal Harvey, who first discovered the circulation of the blood, and who at the time was considered a notorious quack. INDIAN WAR IN FLORIDA. Extract of a Letter dated Tallahassee, February 1, 1836. There has been a fatal error on the part of Government in relation to the strength of these Indians, and the facilities which they have for procrastinating the war. The whole strength of the Indians cannot now be estimated at less than 40 60 effective warriors including the negroes. The country they w ill occupy is about 300 miles long, and about 125 broad ; two-thirds of which (the centre) is covered with a chain of Lakes studded with Islands and almost endless glades, and chequered with lagoons and deep narrow streams, making in all directions into the sea arched over as it were with mats of evergreens and high grass. The part which is out of water, or rather subject to a partial inundation, may be considered þÿ classed as follows: Spots of open pine woods, thick evergreen shrubs and grassy glades, and now and then high and fertile hammocks. '1 lie open pine woods offer an inexhaustible quantity of compty '<r arrow root, and excellent substitute for bt ad, and easily prepared. The high hammocks, a variety of fruits whilst the waters every where are iillud with fish and fowl, and the whole lorest with wild game. Three years ago, when 1 examined this country, 1 met with clans of Indians in towns and at lisheries, who seemed to know nothing about any white people except Spaniards with whom they are intermixed ; the Spaniards having Squaws for wives, and the Indian men and half-breeds engaged as fishermen and sailors. Many of those Indians, I

was told, were excellent sailors, and well acquainted on the coast of Cuba ; that they hud frequently passed in their large canoes at a favorable time from the Keys to that island. From these acts, and the strong partiality tliev have had for these Spanish fishermen, 1 should not he surprised if they are not fed up with the vain hope il finally escaping to some of these West India Islands with ail their negroes. If those Indians are not encompassed on the land side by block-houses, and on the water by armed vessels or boats, so as to break up all communication between them and these
